laws.title: Helmet Mandatory for Two-Wheeler Riders
laws.subtitle: Motor Vehicles Act 1988 §129 — ISI-approved helmets
laws.fullDescription: All two-wheeler riders and pillion passengers must wear ISI-approved helmets on all roads. Children above 4 years must also wear helmets per 2019 amendment.
laws.penalty: ₹1,000 first offense. ₹2,000 subsequent offenses. Possible licence suspension.
exceptions: Sikhs wearing turbans are exempt nationwide
Enclosed three-wheeler drivers

quiz.q: Which group is exempt from helmet laws in India?
quiz.explanation: Sikhs wearing turbans are nationally exempt from motorcycle helmet requirements.

laws.title: Indian Greeting — Namaste and Remove Shoes
laws.subtitle: Namaste is universal; shoes off at homes and temples
laws.fullDescription: 'Namaste' (pressing palms together, slight bow) is the traditional Indian greeting understood across all regions and religions. Handshakes common in urban business. Women may not extend hand — wait for their lead. Remove shoes before entering homes, temples, mosques. Never point feet at someone or a deity — deeply disrespectful.
laws.penalty: Not legal — pointing feet at elders or religious objects causes deep offence.
exceptions: Major cities and Westernised environments have more relaxed norms

quiz.q: What does the traditional greeting 'Namaste' involve?
options: Pressing palms together with slight bow
quiz.explanation: Namaste involves pressing your palms together (anjali mudra) and bowing slightly.

laws.title: Cow Protection Laws — Beef Ban in Multiple States
laws.subtitle: State laws vary — UP, Gujarat, Rajasthan: criminal offences
laws.fullDescription: Cow slaughter is banned in most Indian states due to the cow's sacred status in Hinduism. In states like Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, and Rajasthan, slaughtering a cow (or in some states, even possessing beef) is a serious criminal offence. 'Cow vigilante' groups have attacked people suspected of transporting cattle. Foreign tourists should be aware that carrying beef products through certain states carries real risk.
laws.penalty: UP: up to 10 years imprisonment for cow slaughter. Gujarat: life imprisonment. Rajasthan: 6 months to 5 years.
exceptions: Kerala, West Bengal, and northeastern states allow beef legally
Certain communities with historical exemptions

quiz.q: What is the penalty for cow slaughter in Uttar Pradesh, India?
quiz.explanation: UP's Prevention of Cow Slaughter Act carries up to 10 years imprisonment — one of India's strictest state laws on this matter.

laws.title: Photography Restrictions — Monuments, Military Sites
laws.subtitle: Ancient Monuments Act 1958 — Drones and tripods banned at many sites
laws.fullDescription: Photography inside many of India's protected monuments and UNESCO sites requires a separate fee. Drone flying near historical monuments (including the Taj Mahal, Red Fort) is banned without DGCA permission. Military installations, border areas, and certain government buildings prohibit photography. Tripod photography at many heritage sites requires an additional permit.
laws.penalty: Drone at protected monument without permission: fine and equipment confiscation. Photography in prohibited military area: possible detention.
exceptions: Personal handheld cameras permitted at most monuments
Official press and documentary crews with permits
laws.sourceLabel: Archaeological Survey of India — Photography Rules

quiz.q: Are drones allowed near the Taj Mahal?
options: No — banned without DGCA special permission
quiz.explanation: Drones are banned near the Taj Mahal and most protected Indian monuments without special DGCA (aviation authority) permission.

laws.title: Noise Pollution — India's Growing Urban Problem; NGT Rules
laws.subtitle: National Green Tribunal — Silence zones; Diwali fireworks restrictions
laws.fullDescription: India's National Green Tribunal (NGT) has issued orders restricting noise in designated silence zones (within 100 metres of hospitals, courts, educational institutions, and religious sites). Firecrackers during Diwali are restricted in many cities — Delhi and other cities have banned firecrackers entirely during Diwali to address severe air and noise pollution. Loudspeakers at religious events require police permission and must comply with noise limits (45dB daytime, 55dB nighttime residential). Honking in silence zones carries fines.
laws.penalty: Loudspeaker without permission: fine ₹5,000. Fireworks ban violation: fine + confiscation. Noise in silence zone: fine.
exceptions: Government and police emergency announcements
Licensed events with police permission
laws.sourceLabel: National Green Tribunal — Noise Pollution Rules 2000

quiz.q: What are 'silence zones' in India under noise pollution rules?
options: Areas where all noise is banned
100-metre zones around hospitals, courts, schools, and religious sites where noise limits are strictly enforced
quiz.explanation: India's silence zones extend 100 metres around hospitals, courts, educational institutions, and religious sites — loudspeakers and excessive noise in these areas carry fines under National Green Tribunal rules.

laws.title: Cow Protection Laws — Slaughter Bans and Complex Beef Rules
laws.subtitle: State-level laws — 28 of 28 states have varying cow slaughter restrictions
laws.fullDescription: India has no single national cow slaughter law, but most Indian states have enacted their own bans — some prohibiting all bovine slaughter, others restricting only cows while permitting buffalo. States like Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, and Rajasthan have some of the strictest laws, with sentences up to 10 years. The beef trade and consumption by Muslim and Christian minorities has created significant social tension, and in some cases vigilante 'cow protection' groups have carried out mob violence against suspected beef traders — prompting Supreme Court condemnation. Importing beef into India is broadly restricted under FSSAI regulations, making it effectively unavailable in most of the country.
laws.penalty: Slaughtering a cow in a ban state: up to 10 years imprisonment and heavy fines (varies by state). Transporting cattle for slaughter without permit: 7 years in Uttar Pradesh under the 2020 Prevention of Slaughter Act.
exceptions: Some states permit buffalo slaughter
Kerala and several north-eastern states have fewer restrictions on beef
laws.sourceLabel: Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act & State Cow Protection Laws — India

quiz.q: Which Indian state has some of the strictest cow slaughter laws with up to 10 years imprisonment?
quiz.explanation: Uttar Pradesh's Prevention of Cow Slaughter Act 2020 carries penalties of up to 10 years imprisonment for slaughtering cows — one of the strictest such laws in India.

laws.title: Cow Slaughter and Beef Bans — Vary Sharply by State
laws.subtitle: State Prevention of Cow Slaughter Acts — UP, Gujarat, Haryana: strictest; Kerala, WB, NE: exempt
laws.fullDescription: Cow protection is enshrined in Article 48 of India’s Constitution and implemented through state-level laws that vary enormously. Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Rajasthan operate total bans on cow slaughter and beef possession with the heaviest penalties. Gujarat’s 2017 amendment made cow slaughter punishable by up to life imprisonment. By contrast, Kerala, West Bengal, and the north-eastern states (Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh, Tripura) permit cow slaughter and beef sale. The divergence creates traps for travellers: carrying beef across a state border, ordering a ‘beef’ dish in a mixed state, or transporting cattle can all trigger arrest. Cow vigilante groups operate informally in several states and have been involved in violent incidents; police have been criticised for prosecuting travellers rather than vigilantes.
laws.penalty: Cow slaughter (UP, Gujarat, Haryana): 7 years to life imprisonment + fines up to ₹5 lakh. Beef possession in ban states: up to 10 years imprisonment. Cattle transport without permit: arrest and seizure of vehicle.
exceptions: Kerala, West Bengal, Goa, and the seven north-eastern states permit cow slaughter and beef consumption
Water buffalo meat (‘carabeef’) is legal in most states and is frequently mislabelled as beef in export markets
laws.sourceLabel: State Prevention of Cow Slaughter Acts — Ministry of Home Affairs, India

quiz.q: Which Indian state has one of the strictest cow slaughter laws, punishable by up to life imprisonment?
quiz.explanation: Gujarat’s 2017 amendment to its Animal Preservation Act made cow slaughter punishable by up to life imprisonment — one of the harshest in India. Kerala, Goa, and Mizoram permit cow slaughter.

laws.title: Project Tiger — Tiger Reserves Have Strict Access Rules; Buffer Zones Enforced
laws.subtitle: Wildlife Protection Act 1972 — 54 tiger reserves; core zones closed to tourists
laws.fullDescription: India runs the world's most successful large predator conservation programme — Project Tiger (1973) has grown India's wild tiger population from approximately 1,800 in 1973 to over 3,000 today. India's 54 tiger reserves are divided into core zones (no tourist entry allowed) and buffer zones (limited guided safari entry). The Wildlife Protection Act 1972 makes it a criminal offence to enter core zones, disturb wildlife, or go off designated safari tracks. Permits for buffer zone entry must be booked in advance online — walk-in safaris are not permitted at most reserves. Drone photography in tiger reserves is strictly banned without Wildlife Institute of India approval.
laws.penalty: Entering a tiger reserve core zone without authorisation: up to 7 years imprisonment + ₹25 lakh fine. Drone use: confiscation + criminal charge. Off-track driving: expulsion + fine.
exceptions: Forest Department researchers with Chief Wildlife Warden permission
Anti-poaching patrols and forest guards on official duty
laws.sourceLabel: Project Tiger — National Tiger Conservation Authority

quiz.q: Approximately how many wild tigers does India have today, following Project Tiger's conservation success?
quiz.explanation: India's wild tiger population has grown to over 3,000 — up from approximately 1,800 when Project Tiger launched in 1973. India is home to approximately 75% of the world's remaining wild tigers.

laws.title: Project Tiger — Entering Tiger Reserves Without Permits is a Criminal Offense
laws.subtitle: India's 53 Tiger Reserves have core zones closed to all visitors; wildlife law strictly enforced
laws.fullDescription: India's Wildlife Protection Act (1972) and Project Tiger (launched 1973) created a network of 53 tiger reserves covering 75,000+ km². Each reserve has a 'core zone' (critical tiger habitat) where no human entry is permitted — not even for forest officials without special authorization. 'Buffer zones' allow limited, permit-based eco-tourism with certified naturalist guides. The Tiger Conservation Act (2006) created the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) and mandates relocation of villages from core zones with compensation. Camera traps and satellite collars make tiger movement monitoring highly advanced. Killing a tiger carries mandatory minimum 3 years imprisonment; poaching for body parts (used in traditional Chinese medicine) carries 7 years.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized entry into tiger reserve core zone: fine up to ₹25,000 + 3 years imprisonment. Tiger poaching: 3–7 years mandatory imprisonment + fines. Wildlife trade: similar penalties.
exceptions: NTCA-authorized researchers with specific study permits
Forest department anti-poaching patrols
Emergency medical evacuations
laws.sourceLabel: National Tiger Conservation Authority — Tiger Reserve Rules

quiz.q: How many tiger reserves does India currently have under Project Tiger?
quiz.explanation: India has 53 tiger reserves under Project Tiger as of 2023, covering over 75,000 km² — the result of a conservation program that helped the country's tiger population recover from fewer than 2,000 to over 3,000 individuals.

laws.title: Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) — Religious Criteria for Fast-Track Citizenship Contested
laws.subtitle: India's 2019 CAA fast-tracks citizenship for non-Muslim refugees from three countries
laws.fullDescription: India's Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA, 2019) creates a fast-track citizenship pathway for Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, and Christian refugees from Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan who entered India before December 31, 2014 — explicitly excluding Muslims. Critics argue it violates Article 14 of the Indian Constitution's equal treatment guarantee. The Supreme Court has considered challenges. The CAA triggered massive protests (December 2019 – March 2020) — one of independent India's largest. Over 100 protesters were killed in police clashes. Combined with the National Register of Citizens (NRC), critics feared stateless Muslims. The Modi government implemented CAA rules in March 2024. Several state governments (Kerala, West Bengal) passed resolutions refusing to implement CAA — though implementation is a federal matter.
laws.penalty: CAA is a citizenship benefit law, not a criminal penalty law. Protesters against CAA were charged under NSA, sedition, and riot provisions — with hundreds detained.
exceptions: The CAA does not strip existing citizenship from anyone
Muslims already holding Indian citizenship are unaffected
Tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, and Tripura exempted due to demographic concerns
laws.sourceLabel: Indian Ministry of Home Affairs — Citizenship Amendment Act 2019

quiz.q: Which religious group is explicitly excluded from fast-track citizenship under India's Citizenship Amendment Act?
quiz.explanation: India's Citizenship Amendment Act explicitly excludes Muslims from its fast-track citizenship pathway — which covers Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, and Christian refugees from Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan. Critics argue this religious exclusion violates the Indian Constitution's equality guarantee.

laws.title: India's New Criminal Codes — Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita Replaces 163-Year-Old IPC
laws.subtitle: India replaced its British-era criminal code in 2023; colonial sedition law abolished but 'terrorism' expanded
laws.fullDescription: India enacted three new criminal law codes effective July 2024, replacing laws drafted under British colonial rule. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) replaced the Indian Penal Code (1860). The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure (1898). The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam replaced the Evidence Act (1872). Key changes: the colonial sedition law (Section 124A IPC) was officially abolished — replaced by Section 152 BNS, which criminalizes acts 'endangering sovereignty' with potentially broader scope. Electronic evidence is now admissible. Organized crime and terrorism are defined in the main criminal code. Critics argued the rename was cosmetic — core structures remain. The new codes use Hindi names, symbolically decolonizing the legal system.
laws.penalty: Under BNS: murder — death or life imprisonment. Terrorism — up to life or death penalty. 'Endangering sovereignty' (replacing sedition): up to 7 years. Organized crime: up to life imprisonment.
exceptions: Constitutional rights protections remain — freedom of speech challenges to overly broad provisions still available
Parliamentary privileges for speech in Parliament unchanged
Treaty obligations for specific extraditable offenses follow different procedures
laws.sourceLabel: Indian Ministry of Law — Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023

quiz.q: What did India's Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (2023) officially replace?
options: The Indian Penal Code (1860), a 163-year-old British colonial criminal law
quiz.explanation: India's Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaced the Indian Penal Code of 1860 — a 163-year-old criminal law drafted under British colonial rule by Thomas Macaulay. The replacement was part of a broader decolonization of India's three main criminal law statutes, symbolically replacing British-era names with Sanskrit-derived Hindi names.

laws.title: Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) Controversy
laws.subtitle: India's 2019 citizenship law excludes Muslims from fast-track citizenship, triggering mass protests
laws.fullDescription: India's Citizenship Amendment Act (2019) fast-tracks citizenship for persecuted religious minorities — Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis, and Christians — from Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan. Critically, it excludes Muslims, making it the first Indian law to use religion as a criterion. Critics argued it violated Article 14 of the Constitution (equality before law) and combined with the National Register of Citizens could render millions of Muslim Indians stateless. The CAA triggered nationwide protests — the largest since independence — and violence that killed over 50 in Delhi in February 2020. Rules were finally notified in March 2024, making the law operational.
laws.penalty: Providing false information in CAA applications: 5 years imprisonment. Protests blocking public roads: preventive detention under NSA. Sedition charges (since narrowed by Supreme Court) were used against protest leaders.
exceptions: The CAA does not remove citizenship from existing Indian Muslims
Sri Lankan Tamils, Rohingya, and Tibetans are excluded from CAA benefits
Each state has discretion over NRC implementation
laws.sourceLabel: Indian Ministry of Home Affairs — CAA Rules 2024

quiz.q: Which religious group is notably excluded from India's Citizenship Amendment Act fast-track citizenship?
quiz.explanation: India's CAA fast-tracks citizenship for persecuted minorities from Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan — but explicitly excludes Muslims, making it the first Indian citizenship law to use religion as a criterion and triggering massive nationwide protests.

laws.title: G20 Presidency & Global South Champion
laws.subtitle: India's 2023 G20 summit included the African Union and positioned Modi as leader of the developing world
laws.fullDescription: India's G20 Presidency (December 2022 – November 2023) culminated in the New Delhi Summit of September 2023 — widely considered a diplomatic triumph. India secured the African Union's permanent G20 membership, adding 55 African nations to the forum. Modi positioned India as the voice of the 'Global South' — an alternative pole between the US-led West and China. India's presidency produced a consensus declaration on Ukraine that avoided directly condemning Russia (reflecting India's strategic autonomy). India also launched the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) as a rival to China's Belt and Road Initiative.
laws.penalty: Diplomatic protocol violations at G20 events: sovereign immunity protects heads of state. India's Diplomatic Privileges Act governs foreign mission operations. IMEC infrastructure projects will fall under respective national investment laws.
exceptions: India's 'strategic autonomy' means it is not in any formal bloc — maintaining relations with both Russia and the West
African Union membership in G20 is permanent but decision-making rules remain unchanged
IMEC is an MOU framework — no binding legal obligations yet

quiz.q: What organization did India secure as a permanent G20 member at the 2023 New Delhi Summit?
quiz.explanation: India's G20 Presidency secured the African Union's permanent membership in the G20 at the New Delhi Summit in September 2023 — adding 55 African nations to the forum and strengthening India's position as a champion of the Global South.

laws.title: Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA): Religion-Based Fast-Track Citizenship
laws.subtitle: India's 2019 CAA grants expedited citizenship to non-Muslim refugees from three neighbors — critics call it anti-Muslim discrimination
laws.fullDescription: India's Citizenship Amendment Act (2019) fast-tracks citizenship for Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, and Christian refugees who fled religious persecution from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, and Pakistan before December 31, 2014. Muslims are explicitly excluded. The CAA triggered some of India's largest protests in decades, including the Shaheen Bagh sit-in led by Muslim women. Critics argue that combined with a proposed National Register of Citizens (NRC), the CAA could render Muslim minorities stateless. The Supreme Court upheld the CAA in 2024. The government implemented it via notifications in March 2024, four years after passage.
laws.penalty: No penalty for citizens. Individuals who fail to qualify for NRC in states where it is implemented could face detention in foreigner camps
exceptions: Tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram, and Tripura are excluded from the CAA
Those who entered India before December 31, 2014 qualify for the expedited path
laws.sourceLabel: Indian Ministry of Home Affairs – CAA

quiz.q: Which religion is explicitly excluded from India's Citizenship Amendment Act's fast-track citizenship path?
quiz.explanation: India's Citizenship Amendment Act grants expedited citizenship to refugees of six religions from three neighboring countries — but explicitly excludes Muslims, who face religious persecution in these countries too, which critics say makes the law discriminatory.

laws.title: Farm Laws Repeal: India's Largest Protest Forces Modi to Back Down
laws.subtitle: A year-long farmers' siege of Delhi's borders forced Modi to repeal three farm liberalization laws — the first major policy reversal of his government
laws.fullDescription: In September 2020, the Modi government passed three farm laws intended to liberalize India's agricultural markets — removing mandatory selling through government-regulated markets (APMCs) and allowing direct corporate purchase. Farmers, primarily from Punjab and Haryana, feared the end of Minimum Support Prices would leave them at the mercy of large corporations. From November 2020, hundreds of thousands of farmers blockaded Delhi's highways for over a year in freezing temperatures. The protest became one of the largest in world history. In November 2021 — just before key state elections — Modi announced he would repeal all three laws. The Farmers' Protest was a rare instance of organized civil society forcing a major policy reversal on India's central government.
laws.penalty: Protest participants faced sedition charges, riot accusations, and arrests — over 80 FIRs (First Information Reports) were filed against protest leaders. Charges were later dropped under the repeal agreement
exceptions: The minimum support price (MSP) guarantee demanded by farmers was not legislated — it remains a government policy commitment without legal force
Farmers retained the right to sell through existing APMC markets under the repealed laws' framework
laws.sourceLabel: BBC News – India Farm Laws Repeal

quiz.q: How long did India's farmer protests blocking Delhi's highways last before Modi agreed to repeal the farm laws?
quiz.explanation: The farmers' protests blocking Delhi's major highways lasted over 13 months — from November 2020 to December 2021 — becoming one of the world's largest sustained protest movements and forcing a rare major policy reversal from Modi's government ahead of key state elections.

laws.title: Cow Protection Laws
laws.subtitle: Most Indian states ban cow slaughter — the sacred animal of Hinduism
laws.fullDescription: Cow slaughter is banned in 28 of India's 36 states and union territories under state-level laws. The Constitution of India's Directive Principles (Article 48) directs the state to organize agriculture and prohibit cow slaughter. State laws vary from total bans (including on transport and beef possession) in states like Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan, to regulations only on slaughter in others. The Uttar Pradesh Prevention of Cow Slaughter Act 2020 carries up to 10 years imprisonment. Vigilante 'cow protection' groups (gau rakshak dals) have been linked to violence. Beef consumption is entirely legal in most northeastern states and Kerala.
laws.penalty: UP: 1–10 years imprisonment, fines up to ₹5 lakh; other states: 1–7 years; varies significantly by state
exceptions: Kerala, West Bengal, and most northeastern states permit cow slaughter and beef consumption
Muslim and Christian communities have challenged bans under religious freedom provisions

quiz.q: Which article of India's Constitution directs the state to consider prohibiting cow slaughter?
quiz.explanation: Article 48 of India's Directive Principles of State Policy directs the state to organize agriculture and animal husbandry and prohibit slaughter of cows, calves, and other milch and draught cattle.

laws.title: Right to Information Act
laws.subtitle: India's RTI Act gives citizens the right to demand government documents
laws.fullDescription: India's Right to Information Act (2005) gives every citizen the right to request information held by any public authority within 30 days. The Act covers all three branches of government and public bodies funded by government. An estimated 6 million RTI applications are filed annually — making India's RTI framework one of the world's most active. The Act has been used to expose corruption in public works, food security programs, and land records. However, RTI activists face violence — over 100 have been killed and hundreds assaulted for filing politically inconvenient RTI requests. The 2019 RTI Amendment Act weakened the independence of Information Commissioners, drawing criticism.
laws.penalty: Public Information Officers who fail to provide information: Rs 250/day fine (up to Rs 25,000); serious violations: disciplinary action
exceptions: Information related to national security, cabinet decisions, third-party commercial information, and personal privacy can be withheld
Intelligence agencies are exempt

quiz.q: Approximately how many RTI applications are filed annually in India?
quiz.explanation: An estimated 6 million Right to Information applications are filed across India each year — making it the most actively used transparency law by volume globally, a testament to both the Act's accessibility and the demand for government accountability.

laws.title: Smart Cities Mission Law
laws.subtitle: India's Smart Cities Mission is a federal urban development programme with legal targets
laws.fullDescription: India's Smart Cities Mission (2015) designated 100 cities for rapid infrastructure development using an Area-Based Development model — focusing on a specific area within each city rather than the whole urban area. Cities receive central government funding (Rs 100 crore per year for 5 years) and must implement digital infrastructure (smart meters, CCTV, Wi-Fi), clean energy, and efficient urban transport. The mission is governed by the Smart Cities Mission guidelines under the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. By 2024, over 7,800 projects were completed under the mission. Critics argue the smart cities approach benefits upscale areas while neglecting informal settlements housing most urban poor.
laws.penalty: Cities that fail to meet mission milestones: funding suspended and redistributed to compliant cities
exceptions: Projects in slums and EWS (Economically Weaker Sections) areas receive priority under Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana integration

quiz.q: How many cities were designated under India's Smart Cities Mission?
quiz.explanation: India's Smart Cities Mission, launched in 2015, designated 100 cities for smart infrastructure development. Cities were selected through a competitive process called the 'City Challenge,' with winners receiving central government funding for digital and physical infrastructure upgrades.

laws.title: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act
laws.subtitle: India's comprehensive 2012 child protection law created gender-neutral offenses with mandatory reporting
laws.fullDescription: India's Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012 (amended 2019) is the country's primary legislation protecting children under 18 from sexual abuse and exploitation. The Act: defines multiple offenses (penetrative sexual assault, non-penetrative assault, sexual harassment, use of children for pornography); is gender-neutral (protects all children regardless of gender); creates special POCSO courts for expedited trials; mandates that all cases be tried within one year; requires mandatory reporting — any adult with knowledge of child sexual abuse must report it to police (failure to report is a criminal offense); and establishes child-friendly procedures (in-camera trials, no cross-examination by the accused, support persons). The 2019 amendment increased penalties including death penalty for aggravated penetrative sexual assault of children under 12. Child helpline 1098 is the primary reporting mechanism.
laws.penalty: Penetrative sexual assault: 20 years to life imprisonment; aggravated cases: death penalty; pornography: 5–7 years; failure to report: 6 months imprisonment and/or fine
exceptions: Consensual sexual activity between adolescents within 2 years of age has been interpreted by some courts to require softer application (though legally still an offense)
Medical examinations of child abuse victims are exempt from some evidence rules
Good faith reporting is protected from defamation suits

laws.title: Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) 2019
laws.subtitle: India's CAA created religion-based fast-track citizenship for non-Muslim minorities from three countries
laws.fullDescription: India's Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA), passed December 11, 2019 and implemented with rules issued March 2024, fast-tracks Indian citizenship for Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis, and Christians who entered India from Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan before December 31, 2014. Crucially, Muslims from those countries are excluded. The BJP government argues this protects religious minorities persecuted in Muslim-majority countries. Critics — including the Indian National Congress, civil society organizations, and UN human rights experts — argue the religion-based distinction violates Article 14 of the Indian Constitution (equality before the law) and combined with the proposed National Register of Citizens (NRC), could render millions of Muslim Indians stateless. The CAA triggered massive nationwide protests (December 2019–February 2020), resulting in violent crackdowns. Multiple state governments declared they would not implement it. The Supreme Court has pending constitutional challenges.
laws.penalty: No direct criminal penalties from the CAA itself; the NRC process theoretically would require excluded persons to prove citizenship or face detention/deportation; implementation varies by state
exceptions: Tribally protected areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram, and Tripura are excluded from CAA application
The Inner Line Permit areas have separate provisions
Legal challenges in the Supreme Court may ultimately change implementation

laws.title: CAA Implemented Before 2024 Elections
laws.subtitle: India's citizenship law for religious minorities went into force amid controversy
laws.fullDescription: India's Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA), passed in December 2019, was implemented by notification in March 2024 — just before general elections. The law offers expedited citizenship to persecuted religious minorities (Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis, Christians) from Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan — but explicitly excludes Muslims. Critics argued this discriminates on religious grounds and, combined with a potential National Register of Citizens, could render stateless millions of Muslims unable to prove citizenship. Massive protests erupted in 2019-2020 (Delhi riots). The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights called it discriminatory. The Supreme Court has received challenges but upheld the law's basic validity.
laws.penalty: Fraudulent citizenship application: up to 5 years imprisonment under Citizenship Act. Entering India without valid documentation: up to 5 years imprisonment.
exceptions: CAA citizenship path is optional — existing citizenship laws unaffected
Tribal areas in Northeast excluded from CAA application due to Inner Line Permit protections

quiz.q: Which religious group is explicitly NOT included in India's Citizenship Amendment Act?
quiz.explanation: The CAA offers expedited citizenship to persecuted religious minorities from Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan — but explicitly excludes Muslims, which critics argue violates India's secular constitutional principles.

laws.title: UAPA and the Shrinking Space for Dissent
laws.subtitle: India's anti-terror law has been used against journalists, activists, and academics
laws.fullDescription: India's Unlawful Activities Prevention Act (UAPA), amended significantly in 2019, allows designation of individuals (not just organizations) as 'terrorists' without trial. It permits detention without bail for up to 180 days before charges, and bail is extremely difficult to obtain. The law has been criticized by UN human rights experts and opposition parties for use against journalists (Siddique Kappan), academics (Stan Swamy, who died in custody), and activists (the Bhima Koregaon 16). The Supreme Court has struggled to provide consistent bail standards. Separately, India's new criminal code (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, effective July 2024) replaced the colonial-era IPC but retained and expanded some sedition-like provisions under different language.
laws.penalty: Designated terrorist under UAPA: bail virtually impossible — up to life imprisonment or death for terrorist acts. Sedition-equivalent under BNS: up to 7 years.
exceptions: Terrorism charges require NIA (National Investigation Agency) approval
High Court and Supreme Court retain habeas corpus jurisdiction — though used sparingly in UAPA cases
Diplomatic and foreign press not typically targeted

quiz.q: What controversial power did India's 2019 UAPA amendment add?
options: Authority to ban political parties without judicial review
The ability to designate individuals (not just organizations) as 'terrorists' without trial
Power to conduct mass surveillance without court orders
Authority to revoke citizenship of suspected terrorists
quiz.explanation: The 2019 UAPA amendment allowed the Indian government to designate individual people (not just organizations) as terrorists — enabling the labeling and effective imprisonment of journalists, academics, and activists without criminal conviction.

laws.title: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act
laws.subtitle: DPDPA 2023 establishes India's first comprehensive data privacy law
laws.fullDescription: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDPA) 2023 creates a framework for processing digital personal data. Data fiduciaries (companies) must obtain valid consent, provide notice about data use, ensure data accuracy, and delete data after its purpose is fulfilled. The Data Protection Board adjudicates complaints. Significant data fiduciaries (large platforms) face additional obligations including data audits and impact assessments. Cross-border data transfers require government approval for specified countries on a whitelist basis.
laws.penalty: Breach of data security obligations: up to ₹250 crore (~$30 million) per incident. Breach of children's data rules: up to ₹200 crore. Non-compliance with Board orders: up to ₹150 crore. Providing false information to Board: up to ₹10,000
exceptions: Personal data processed for national security and law enforcement exempt
Research, archiving, and statistical purposes have some exemptions
Household processing of personal data by individuals is exempt
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology

quiz.q: What is the maximum fine under India's DPDPA for a data security breach?
quiz.explanation: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 sets the maximum financial penalty at ₹250 crore (approximately $30 million) per incident of data security breach.

laws.title: India's Electoral Bonds System Struck Down
laws.subtitle: Supreme Court rules anonymous political funding scheme unconstitutional
laws.fullDescription: India's Electoral Bond Scheme (2018) allowed companies and individuals to purchase special bonds anonymously from the State Bank of India, which political parties could then cash. Critics argued it enabled secret corporate donations to ruling parties. In February 2024, India's Supreme Court struck down the scheme unanimously as unconstitutional, ruling it violated citizens' right to information about political funding. The Court ordered SBI to disclose all electoral bond purchasers and recipients. The scheme had channeled over ₹16,000 crore ($1.9 billion) in donations, with the BJP receiving the largest share.
laws.penalty: Political financing violations under Representation of People Act: disqualification from office and fines. Foreign political donations: up to 5 years imprisonment. Bribery through political channels: up to 7 years. Post-ruling: concealing electoral bond information from court: contempt of court
exceptions: Small donations under ₹20,000 don't require donor disclosure
Donations through cheque and digital means under ₹20,000 have simplified disclosure
Political parties retain exemption from income tax on donations received

quiz.q: What did India's Supreme Court rule about the Electoral Bond Scheme in 2024?
options: It was unconstitutional as it violated citizens' right to information about political funding
It was legal but needed amendments
It only applied to foreign donors
quiz.explanation: India's Supreme Court unanimously struck down the Electoral Bond Scheme in February 2024, ruling it unconstitutional for violating citizens' right to information — ordering full disclosure of all bond purchasers and recipients, which revealed billions in secret corporate political donations.

laws.title: India's Space Policy and Commercial Launch Regulations
laws.subtitle: India's ISRO opens space sector to private companies
laws.fullDescription: India's revised space policy (2023) and the establishment of IN-SPACe (Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre) opened India's space sector to private companies for the first time. Chandrayaan-3 became the first spacecraft to land near the Moon's south pole in August 2023 — a major achievement. Private companies like Skyroot Aerospace launched India's first private rocket. The Space Activities Bill (awaiting final passage) will create comprehensive licensing and liability framework. India's ISRO competes for commercial launches and the country is developing a space tourism and satellite internet sector.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized space launch: criminal prosecution under forthcoming Space Activities Act. Violating radio frequency allocation for satellites: severe fines from DoT. Space debris causing damage: liability under proposed Space Activities Bill. Unauthorized image capture from space of sensitive areas: national security prosecution
exceptions: Academic nanosatellite programs at IITs and research institutions have simplified IN-SPACe approval
Government space projects bypass private sector authorization requirements
International collaborative missions approved by ISRO have expedited clearance

quiz.q: What historic lunar achievement did India's Chandrayaan-3 accomplish in August 2023?
options: First spacecraft to return lunar samples
First spacecraft to land near the Moon's south pole
quiz.explanation: India's Chandrayaan-3 became the first spacecraft from any country to successfully land near the Moon's south pole in August 2023 — a historic achievement that made India the fourth country to land on the Moon and the first to reach this scientifically important polar region.

laws.title: Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023
laws.subtitle: India enacted comprehensive data privacy law covering 1.4 billion people
laws.fullDescription: India's Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act 2023 established the country's first comprehensive data privacy framework. The Act creates consent-based data processing rights, appoints a Data Protection Board, and imposes obligations on data fiduciaries (businesses) to protect personal data and report breaches. Significant data fiduciaries with large-scale processing must comply with additional obligations. Cross-border data transfers require government notification. The Act exempts government data processing for national security. Rules implementing the Act were under development through 2024-2025. Financial penalties can reach ₹250 crore (~$30 million) per violation.
laws.penalty: Data breach failures: up to ₹250 crore per instance; processing children's data without consent: up to ₹200 crore
exceptions: Research, archival, and statistical purposes with appropriate safeguards
Government processing for national security and law enforcement
laws.sourceLabel: India Ministry of Electronics and IT

quiz.q: What body does India's DPDP Act create to handle data protection complaints?
quiz.explanation: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 established a Data Protection Board of India to adjudicate complaints and enforce data protection obligations.

laws.title: New Criminal Codes Replace 160-Year-Old British Laws
laws.subtitle: India replaced its colonial-era criminal codes with Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita in 2024
laws.fullDescription: India replaced its three major colonial-era criminal laws in 2024: the Indian Penal Code (1860) became the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS); the Code of Criminal Procedure (1973) became the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS); and the Indian Evidence Act (1872) became the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA). The new codes retained most substantive provisions but added organized crime, terrorism provisions, and electronic evidence handling. The sedition law was replaced with a broader 'acts against sovereignty' provision. 'Hit and run' criminal liability was enhanced. The transition created administrative challenges as courts adjusted to new section numbering.
laws.penalty: Organized crime causing death: life imprisonment or death; terrorism under new BNS: death or life imprisonment; hit and run causing death: up to 10 years
exceptions: Transitional provisions allow old code cases to continue under old provisions
Special courts for specific offenses retain their parallel jurisdiction

quiz.q: What replaced India's Indian Penal Code (1860) in 2024?
quiz.explanation: India's 2024 criminal law overhaul replaced the colonial-era Indian Penal Code (1860) with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), along with replacing the Code of Criminal Procedure and Indian Evidence Act with new Indian-named equivalents.

laws.title: Citizenship Amendment Act and NRC Controversy
laws.subtitle: India's 2019 CAA offered citizenship to persecuted minorities but excluded Muslims
laws.fullDescription: India's Citizenship Amendment Act (2019) fast-tracked citizenship for persecuted Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, and Christian refugees from Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan — but explicitly excluded Muslims. The law was criticized as discriminatory and unconstitutional. Nationwide protests in 2019-2020 (the largest in independent India's history for this issue) were suppressed, with casualties in Delhi. The rules for CAA implementation were notified in March 2024, finally implementing the law. When combined with proposed National Register of Citizens (NRC) exercises, critics warned stateless Muslims could be targeted. The Supreme Court's review of CAA's constitutionality continued.
laws.penalty: Providing false documentation for CAA citizenship: criminal fraud; protests against CAA violating Section 144 orders: arrest
exceptions: Muslims and other excluded groups can use existing citizenship pathways
Persons born in India retain citizenship regardless of religion

quiz.q: Which religious group does India's Citizenship Amendment Act explicitly exclude from fast-tracked citizenship?
quiz.explanation: India's Citizenship Amendment Act explicitly excludes Muslims from fast-tracked citizenship for persecuted minorities from Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan — a distinction that critics argue violates India's secular constitutional principles.

laws.title: India Digital Personal Data Protection Act
laws.subtitle: India enacts its first comprehensive data privacy law
laws.fullDescription: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDP Act) was passed in August 2023 after years of deliberation. It establishes a Data Protection Board to adjudicate complaints, creates rights for data principals (individuals) including access, correction, and deletion, and requires data fiduciaries (organizations) to process data only for lawful purposes with valid consent. Significant consent for data processing, breach notification obligations, and a new regulatory board are central features. Rules under the Act were being finalized as of 2025.
laws.penalty: Fines up to Rs 250 crore (approximately $30 million USD) per violation
exceptions: State processing for national security
Research, journalistic, and statistical purposes
Processing of publicly available data
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Electronics and IT India

quiz.q: What body does India's DPDP Act establish to adjudicate data protection complaints?
quiz.explanation: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act establishes the Data Protection Board as the adjudicatory body for data privacy complaints.

laws.title: India Telecom Act 2023
laws.subtitle: India overhauls telecommunications law after 138 years
laws.fullDescription: India's Telecommunications Act 2023 replaced the Indian Telegraph Act of 1885, comprehensively modernizing the legal framework for telecommunications. The new law addresses spectrum allocation and assignment, licensing of telecom services, interception and surveillance powers, and cybersecurity obligations for providers. It also enables satellite broadband services under a unified licensing framework. The law retains broad government interception powers, which civil liberty groups argued lack sufficient judicial oversight.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed spectrum use: fines up to Rs 5 crore per day; unauthorized interception: criminal penalties; violations of security directives: license cancellation
exceptions: Government and defense communications
Emergency communications during disasters
Small community radio stations below power thresholds

quiz.q: What previous telecommunications law did India's Telecom Act 2023 replace?
quiz.explanation: India's Telecom Act 2023 replaced the Indian Telegraph Act of 1885 — a 138-year-old colonial-era law — comprehensively modernizing India's telecommunications legal framework.

laws.title: India New Criminal Laws — IPC Replacement
laws.subtitle: India overhauls 163-year-old colonial criminal code
laws.fullDescription: India enacted three new criminal laws in 2023 replacing the Indian Penal Code (1860), the Code of Criminal Procedure (1973), and the Indian Evidence Act (1872) — three colonial-era laws. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam came into force on July 1, 2024. Key changes include: organized crime as a distinct offense, specific terrorism provisions, modernized electronic evidence rules, and a new offense of terrorism. Critics noted that sedition was removed but replaced with broader state security offenses.
laws.penalty: The new laws modernize existing penalties; organized crime: up to life imprisonment; new terrorism offenses: up to life; electronic fraud: new specific penalties
exceptions: Cases filed under the old IPC before July 1, 2024 continue under the old law
Military courts retain separate jurisdiction
State-level offenses follow state legislation

quiz.q: How old was the Indian Penal Code that was replaced by the new criminal laws in 2024?
quiz.explanation: India's Indian Penal Code dated from 1860 — making it 163 years old when replaced on July 1, 2024 by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, itself a product of British colonial governance.

laws.title: Digital Personal Data Protection Act
laws.subtitle: India's comprehensive data privacy legislation
laws.fullDescription: India enacted the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, establishing a framework for processing personal data of Indian citizens. The law requires consent for data processing, mandates data fiduciaries to maintain accuracy and security, gives citizens rights to access and correct their data, establishes a Data Protection Board to adjudicate complaints, restricts processing of children's data, and imposes restrictions on transferring data to certain foreign countries. Significant processing entities will be classified as Significant Data Fiduciaries with additional obligations.
laws.penalty: Data breaches can result in fines up to ₹250 crore (approximately USD 30 million); Significant Data Fiduciaries face penalties up to ₹500 crore for systemic violations
exceptions: Processing for state security and law enforcement has broad exemptions
Personal or household data processing not covered
Research, archiving, and statistical purposes have modified requirements
Processing by the state government for provision of subsidies and benefits is exempt
laws.sourceLabel: Digital India - Ministry of Electronics and IT

quiz.q: What body adjudicates complaints and imposes penalties under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act?
quiz.explanation: India's DPDP Act establishes a Data Protection Board as the adjudicatory body for complaints, appeals, and penalty decisions under the legislation.

laws.title: Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA)
laws.subtitle: India's religious basis for fast-track citizenship for non-Muslim refugees
laws.fullDescription: India's Citizenship Amendment Act creates a fast-track citizenship pathway for Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, and Christian immigrants from Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan who entered India before December 31, 2014. The law explicitly excludes Muslims from this pathway. Critics including the UN Human Rights Office argued the religious exclusion violates India's secular constitution. The government defends it as providing refuge to religious minorities persecuted in those specific Muslim-majority countries. The CAA triggered massive protests with concerns about combined impact with a National Register of Citizens.
laws.penalty: Fraudulent CAA citizenship applications carry criminal liability; individuals who do not qualify but claim CAA status face deportation
exceptions: The CAA applies to six specific non-Muslim religious groups from three specified countries only
Tribal areas in some northeastern states are excluded from CAA application
Persons already Indian citizens are unaffected

quiz.q: Which three countries does India's Citizenship Amendment Act specifically cover for its fast-track pathway?
quiz.explanation: India's Citizenship Amendment Act creates fast-track citizenship specifically for non-Muslim immigrants from Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Bangladesh — three neighboring countries where Muslim-majority governments could persecute the specified religious minorities.

laws.title: New Criminal Codes (BNS, BNSS, BSA)
laws.subtitle: India's replacement of colonial-era criminal laws
laws.fullDescription: India replaced three British colonial-era criminal laws with new Indian codes: the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) replacing the Indian Penal Code of 1860, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) replacing the Code of Criminal Procedure, and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) replacing the Evidence Act. The new codes introduced trial timelines, updated definitions of crimes, added new offenses including organized crime and terrorism, modified bail provisions, introduced electronic summoning, and removed some colonial-era provisions deemed obsolete. Critics questioned whether the rebranding represented substantive reform.
laws.penalty: New BNS provisions create updated penalty structures; organized crime carries up to life imprisonment; terrorism offenses include death penalty; new economic offense provisions carry enhanced financial penalties
exceptions: Offenses committed before the new codes took effect are prosecuted under the old codes
International treaties establish specific procedures that override domestic code provisions
Juvenile offenders are covered by separate juvenile justice legislation

quiz.q: What British colonial law did India's Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) replace?
options: The Code of Civil Procedure of 1908
quiz.explanation: India's Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) replaced the Indian Penal Code of 1860, a colonial-era criminal law that had been the foundation of India's criminal justice system for 163 years — part of a three-law package replacing the core of India's British-era criminal legal framework.

laws.title: India Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (New Criminal Code)
laws.subtitle: Replacing British-era IPC with modernized criminal law
laws.fullDescription: India replaced its 163-year-old Indian Penal Code (IPC) with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) on July 1, 2024. The new code retained most IPC provisions but added new offenses including organized crime, terrorism, and crimes against children, while removing the colonial-era offense of sedition (Section 124A). The BNS was accompanied by new procedural codes: the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (replacing CrPC) and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (replacing the Evidence Act). Electronic evidence rules were significantly modernized.
laws.penalty: The BNS introduced community service as a new penalty option. Maximum penalties increased for offenses against women and children, with gang rape now carrying mandatory death or life imprisonment.
exceptions: Pending cases under the IPC continue under the old code until conclusion
States that had not adopted IPC amendments retain their own criminal law variants for state offenses

quiz.q: On what date did India's new criminal code (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita) come into effect?
quiz.explanation: India's Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) came into effect on July 1, 2024, replacing the Indian Penal Code that had been in force since 1860 during British colonial rule, in one of the most significant legal reforms in India's history.

laws.title: India Citizenship Amendment Act Implementation
laws.subtitle: CAA finally implemented providing citizenship path for religious minorities
laws.fullDescription: India's Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA, passed 2019) was finally implemented through gazette notification in March 2024, just before the general elections. The CAA creates an expedited citizenship path for Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis, and Christians who fled religious persecution from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, and Pakistan before December 2014 — but explicitly excludes Muslims. Critics argued the exclusion violated India's secular constitution; supporters said it addressed religious persecution in Muslim-majority countries. Protests and court challenges followed implementation.
laws.penalty: Providing false information in a CAA citizenship application: imprisonment up to 5 years and loss of citizenship if granted. Officials who grant citizenship without verifying persecution claims face departmental action.
exceptions: Tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram, and Tripura exempt from CAA's application under Schedule VI of the Constitution
Persons holding valid visas or long-term residency permits subject to normal naturalization rather than CAA

quiz.q: Which religion is notably excluded from the Citizenship Amendment Act's expedited citizenship pathway?
quiz.explanation: The Citizenship Amendment Act explicitly excludes Muslims from its expedited citizenship pathway for persecuted religious minorities from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, and Pakistan — a key source of controversy, with critics arguing this religious exclusion violates India's secular constitutional principles.

laws.title: India 2024 General Elections: BJP Coalition Government
laws.subtitle: Modi wins third term but loses outright majority
laws.fullDescription: India held its 18th general elections in April-June 2024, resulting in Prime Minister Modi's BJP winning 240 seats — short of the 272 needed for an outright majority in the 543-seat Lok Sabha. Modi formed a coalition government with NDA (National Democratic Alliance) partners, including TDP (Andhra Pradesh) and JDU (Bihar). The opposition INDIA alliance (Congress-led) performed better than 2019. Modi was sworn in for a historic third consecutive term, but coalition dependency created new political dynamics, with regional parties gaining leverage.
laws.penalty: Electoral violations under India's Representation of the People Act: imprisonment up to 5 years for serious offenses. Booth capturing and voter intimidation: imprisonment up to 3 years.
exceptions: Members of Parliament retain immunity for speeches and votes in Parliament under Article 105 of the Constitution
Election Commission officials who conduct polls in good faith are protected from civil liability for procedural decisions

quiz.q: How many Lok Sabha seats did BJP win in India's 2024 general elections?
quiz.explanation: BJP won 240 Lok Sabha seats in India's 2024 general elections — falling short of the 272 required for a simple majority in the 543-seat house. This required Modi to form a coalition NDA government with regional allies including TDP and JDU, giving regional parties new leverage in national politics.

laws.title: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (New Penal Code)
laws.subtitle: India replaces 163-year-old Indian Penal Code with new criminal laws
laws.fullDescription: India enacted the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), replacing the Indian Penal Code of 1860, along with two companion laws (Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita replacing CrPC, and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam replacing the Evidence Act). The new codes introduced video trial provisions, electronic evidence rules, updated sedition definitions, and mandatory timelines for trials. Critics noted the sedition equivalent (Section 152) was retained in modified form.
laws.penalty: Penalties broadly retained from IPC but reorganised; new organised crime sections with 7 years to life; sedition equivalent: up to 7 years
exceptions: Juvenile justice continues under separate Children's Act
Military personnel subject to parallel Armed Forces laws

quiz.q: What historic law did India's Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replace?
quiz.explanation: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaced the Indian Penal Code of 1860, which had been in force for 163 years, as part of a comprehensive reform of India's colonial-era criminal justice laws.

laws.title: Electoral Bonds Supreme Court Ruling and Ban
laws.subtitle: India's Supreme Court strikes down anonymous electoral funding scheme
laws.fullDescription: India's Supreme Court unanimously struck down the Electoral Bond scheme, which had allowed anonymous donations to political parties through bonds purchased from the State Bank of India. The court ruled it violated voters' right to information about political funding. The government was ordered to disclose all bond purchases and the political parties that received them, revealing major corporate donors.
laws.penalty: Political parties that received electoral bonds were not penalised — future anonymous political funding now prohibited with criminal penalties for circumvention
exceptions: Existing bonds converted to disclosed donations under court-ordered amnesty
Small political donations under ₹20,000 continue under existing simplified cash rules

quiz.q: What right did India's Supreme Court say the Electoral Bond scheme violated?
options: Voters' right to information about political funding
quiz.explanation: India's Supreme Court ruled that the Electoral Bond scheme violated voters' fundamental right to information about who was funding political parties — transparency being essential to democratic accountability.

laws.title: Space Economy Policy and ISRO Privatisation Framework
laws.subtitle: India opens space sector to private companies
laws.fullDescription: India enacted the Space Activities Act and Space Economy Policy, creating a legal framework for private companies to launch rockets, build satellites, and develop space infrastructure. IN-SPACe (Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre) received expanded powers to authorise private launches. Companies like Agnikul, Skyroot, and Pixxel received licences. India targeted a $100 billion space economy by 2040.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed space launches: criminal prosecution and licence disqualification; satellite spectrum violations: TRAI penalties
exceptions: Academic research satellites under 1 kg cubesat size receive simplified authorisation
Defence space activities managed under separate MoD framework with national security classification

quiz.q: What is the name of India's body authorising private space company launches?
quiz.explanation: IN-SPACe (Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre) is the body created to authorise and promote private sector participation in India's space sector — a key part of opening up the sector that ISRO had previously monopolised.

laws.title: Make in India 2.0 and Production Linked Incentives
laws.subtitle: India's PLI scheme drives manufacturing expansion
laws.fullDescription: India expanded its Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme across 14 sectors including semiconductors, electric vehicles, pharmaceuticals, textiles, and food processing. The second-generation PLI 2.0 offered enhanced incentives for companies that achieved export targets and used higher domestic value-added content. India attracted Apple iPhone production, solar module manufacturing, and major EV investments.
laws.penalty: PLI recipients that fail to achieve minimum sales thresholds: pro-rated incentive reduction; fraudulent production claims: criminal prosecution and full clawback
exceptions: Small and medium enterprises have separate Modified PLI with lower entry requirements
R&D manufacturing that doesn't yet have commercial sales receives pre-production support grants

quiz.q: How many sectors does India's expanded PLI scheme cover?
quiz.explanation: India expanded its Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme across 14 sectors — a comprehensive manufacturing incentive programme designed to make India a global manufacturing hub across industries from smartphones to pharmaceuticals.

laws.title: India Digital India Act and AI Governance Framework
laws.subtitle: Replacing IT Act 2000 with comprehensive digital law
laws.fullDescription: India enacted the Digital India Act 2025, replacing the Information Technology Act 2000 with a comprehensive framework for the digital economy. The law establishes the Digital India Authority as unified regulator replacing fragmented oversight, creates a Data Protection Board (building on the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023) with enhanced enforcement powers including sector-specific fines up to 2.5% of global turnover, establishes AI Governance Standards through the Bureau of Indian Standards, mandates AI system registration for high-risk applications in healthcare, finance, and law enforcement, requires all significant social media platforms to appoint resident grievance officers, and introduces the India Digital Public Infrastructure Fund supporting UPI, DigiLocker, and Aadhaar expansion. The law explicitly protects India's 'digital public good' stack from proprietary lock-in.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized data processing: ₹500 crore fine; high-risk AI deployment without registration: ₹250 crore; platform non-compliance with grievance officer requirement: ₹100 crore
exceptions: Individual users processing personal data for household purposes exempt
Government datasets for national security exempt from Data Protection Board oversight
Research institutions with ethics board approval have modified framework
laws.sourceLabel: India Ministry of Electronics and IT

quiz.q: What landmark Indian technology law from 2000 does the Digital India Act 2025 replace?
quiz.explanation: India's Digital India Act 2025 replaces the Information Technology Act 2000 — a 25-year-old law that had become inadequate for regulating the modern digital economy including social media, AI, and digital payments.

laws.title: India Space Economy Policy and Commercial Space Launch Act
laws.subtitle: Opening India's space sector to private enterprise
laws.fullDescription: India enacted the Space Activities and Commercial Space Economy Development Act 2025, opening the Indian space sector to private companies following the Indian Space Policy 2023. The law creates IN-SPACe (Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Centre) as the single-window regulatory authority for private space activities, establishes liability frameworks for commercial launch operators, provides 10-year tax holidays for space manufacturing facilities, creates the India Space Innovation Fund with ₹10,000 crore for private space startups, mandates that ISRO transfer technology to qualified Indian private companies for rocket and satellite production, and establishes the India-US Space Technology Partnership facilitating bilateral space cooperation.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized satellite launch: ₹500 crore fine plus criminal prosecution; space debris creation through negligent operation: unlimited liability; IN-SPACe authorization fraud: 20 years imprisonment
exceptions: Student university satellite projects under 1kg have simplified authorization
Government defense satellite programmes governed under separate security framework
International satellite launch contracts under bilateral agreements have modified IN-SPACe requirements

quiz.q: What is the name of India's single-window regulatory authority for private space activities created by the 2025 Space Activities Act?
quiz.explanation: IN-SPACe (Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Centre) was established as the single-window regulatory authority for private space activities in India — a dedicated body separate from ISRO designed to facilitate India's commercial space ecosystem.

laws.title: Electoral Bond Scheme Abolition and Campaign Finance Reform Act
laws.subtitle: Supreme Court-mandated political funding transparency
laws.fullDescription: Following the Supreme Court of India's unanimous ruling striking down the Electoral Bond Scheme as unconstitutional, Parliament enacted new campaign finance legislation establishing transparent donor disclosure requirements for all political parties. The law mandates real-time online disclosure of donations above 20,000 rupees, prohibits anonymous corporate donations, and establishes an independent Election Finance Commission to audit party accounts.
laws.penalty: Political parties that accept anonymous donations above the threshold face deregistration. Corporate officials who make illegal political donations face fines up to three times the donation amount and up to three years imprisonment.
exceptions: Individual donations below 20,000 rupees remain anonymous to protect small donors
Religious and charitable organizations are prohibited from making political donations regardless of amount

quiz.q: What prompted India's Electoral Bond Scheme Abolition Act?
options: A Supreme Court ruling striking it down as unconstitutional
quiz.explanation: The Supreme Court of India unanimously struck down the Electoral Bond Scheme as unconstitutional, prompting Parliament to enact new transparent campaign finance legislation.

laws.title: Modi Third Term Governance and Opposition Management Act
laws.subtitle: NDA coalition management after weaker mandate
laws.fullDescription: Prime Minister Narendra Modi's BJP won a third term in 2024 but with a weaker mandate requiring greater dependence on coalition partners. The resulting legislation reflects more compromise, including greater state-level fiscal autonomy, modified agricultural policy after previous farm law protests, and revised approach to caste reservation policies in response to coalition partners' demands. The law also addresses opposition concerns about electoral bond transparency.
laws.penalty: Officials who interfere with constitutionally protected reservation rights face disciplinary action and civil liability. Electoral finance violations carry up to five years imprisonment.
exceptions: Union territories under direct central administration retain centralized fiscal arrangements
Emergency public works under natural disaster conditions can bypass normal procurement requirements

quiz.q: What term does Modi's 2024 election victory represent for him as Prime Minister?
quiz.explanation: Modi's 2024 election win was his third consecutive term as Prime Minister, though the BJP needed greater coalition support than in previous elections, requiring more political compromise.

laws.title: Space Economy and Satellite Privatization Act
laws.subtitle: Opening Indian space to private companies
laws.fullDescription: India enacted landmark space legislation privatizing its space sector and opening it to Indian private companies following the success of ISRO's Chandrayaan-3 lunar landing. The law creates the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Centre (IN-SPACe) as a regulatory body, allows private launch vehicles, enables satellite constellation development, creates a commercial launch site licensing framework, and establishes liability rules for private space activities.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized satellite launches without IN-SPACe approval carry up to seven years imprisonment. Space debris creation from non-compliant operations carries civil liability without limitation.
exceptions: ISRO retains its government space program with separate operational rules from the commercial sector
Small student satellites from universities receive simplified licensing under an educational space program

quiz.q: What historic achievement did India's Chandrayaan-3 mission accomplish in August 2023?
options: First Indian satellite to reach Mars
Soft-landed near the Moon's south pole — a global first
Docked with the International Space Station
Deployed a lunar rover that operated for six years
quiz.explanation: India's Chandrayaan-3 became the first spacecraft to soft-land near the Moon's south pole in August 2023, making India only the fourth country to achieve a successful lunar landing. The south pole was historically significant as a previously unreached area with potential water ice deposits.

laws.title: Personal Data Protection and Digital Regulation Act
laws.subtitle: India's comprehensive data privacy framework
laws.fullDescription: India enacted the Digital Personal Data Protection Act after years of delays, creating India's first comprehensive data privacy law. The law establishes consent requirements for data processing, creates rights to access, correction, and erasure, restricts cross-border data transfers to approved countries, creates a Data Protection Board for enforcement, and establishes special provisions protecting children's data.
laws.penalty: Data breaches that are not reported within the required timeframe carry fines up to INR 250 crore. Data processing without proper consent carries fines up to INR 50 crore. Government violations are subject to separate accountability mechanisms.
exceptions: National security and law enforcement data processing is exempt from most privacy requirements
Small entities below a revenue threshold have a two-year grace period for compliance
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Electronics and IT India

quiz.q: What special category of protection does India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act provide for?
quiz.explanation: India's data protection law includes special provisions for children's data, requiring parental or guardian consent for processing data of minors and prohibiting behavioral tracking and targeted advertising to children.

laws.title: India Uniform Civil Code Implementation Framework Act
laws.subtitle: Personal Law Reform and Secular Civil Law
laws.fullDescription: Establishes a framework for implementing a Uniform Civil Code as envisioned by the Constitution's Directive Principles, following Uttarakhand's pioneering state-level UCC. The law creates a national framework for uniform laws governing marriage, divorce, inheritance, and adoption applicable to all citizens regardless of religion. It exempts tribal communities under the Fifth and Sixth Schedules and creates consultation mechanisms for religious communities.
laws.penalty: Administrative penalties for officials failing to implement UCC procedures; compensation for victims of discriminatory personal law application
exceptions: Tribal communities under Fifth and Sixth Schedules retain customary laws
Existing marriages and adoptions under previous law remain valid

quiz.q: Which Indian state pioneered implementing a Uniform Civil Code before the national framework?
quiz.explanation: Uttarakhand pioneered implementing a Uniform Civil Code at the state level before India's national framework act.

laws.title: India Semiconductor Mission and TATA Electronics Fab Support Act
laws.subtitle: Chip Manufacturing Domestic Production Law
laws.fullDescription: Establishes India's framework for domestic semiconductor manufacturing following approval of the first Indian semiconductor fabs. The law provides 50% capital subsidies for semiconductor fabs, creates the India Semiconductor Mission with Rs 76,000 crore allocation, establishes the Semiconductor Laboratory modernization, supports TATA Electronics and Micron fab construction in Gujarat, and mandates chip content in government electronics procurement.
laws.penalty: Subsidy clawback for companies failing production milestones; criminal prosecution for technology misappropriation
exceptions: Display manufacturing has separate support program
Assembly, testing, and packaging facilities have modified support structure

quiz.q: In which Indian state are the first domestic semiconductor fabs being constructed?
quiz.explanation: India's first semiconductor fabs, including TATA Electronics and Micron facilities, are being constructed in Gujarat under the Semiconductor Mission.

laws.title: India NDA Coalition Governance and Economic Agenda Act
laws.subtitle: Third Narendra Modi Term Policy Framework Law
laws.fullDescription: Establishes PM Modi's third term governance priorities after the BJP lost its outright majority and required NDA coalition partners. The law implements the coalition agreement balancing BJP priorities with Nitish Kumar (JDU) and Chandrababu Naidu (TDP) demands, creates special status frameworks for Bihar and Andhra Pradesh, establishes the Viksit Bharat 2047 roadmap implementation, and maintains economic reform momentum.
laws.penalty: Coalition stability mechanisms; parliamentary confidence requirements for major policy changes
exceptions: National security decisions retain PM authority
Foreign policy maintained as central government prerogative

quiz.q: What two coalition parties required special state concessions in Modi's third-term coalition?
quiz.explanation: Nitish Kumar's JDU representing Bihar and Chandrababu Naidu's TDP representing Andhra Pradesh received special state concessions in the BJP coalition.

laws.title: Delimitation Commission and Electoral Representation Shift
laws.subtitle: Southern States Fear Loss of Parliamentary Seats
laws.fullDescription: India's scheduled delimitation of parliamentary constituencies based on updated census data could significantly reduce the number of seats for southern states, which have achieved lower population growth through successful family planning. Southern states argue this penalizes development and threatens federal balance of power.
laws.penalty: No direct penalty; political representation consequences
exceptions: Constitutional provisions for delimitation
Transitional freezes on seat allocation

quiz.q: Why do southern Indian states fear delimitation?
options: Loss of parliamentary seats due to lower population growth
quiz.explanation: Southern states with lower population growth due to successful family planning could lose parliamentary seats under a population-based delimitation.

laws.title: BJP Loses Majority; Modi Forms Coalition Government
laws.subtitle: 2024 Election Results Force Alliance Dependencies
laws.fullDescription: India's 2024 general elections saw the BJP lose its outright parliamentary majority for the first time under Modi, winning around 240 seats rather than the 272 needed for majority. Modi formed his third government relying on coalition partners including the TDP and JDU. The opposition INDIA alliance performed better than polls predicted.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; democratic election outcome
exceptions: Coalition agreement requirements
Parliamentary confidence requirements

quiz.q: What was significant about the BJP's 2024 Indian election result?
options: They lost their outright parliamentary majority for the first time under Modi
quiz.explanation: The BJP lost its outright majority in 2024, forcing Modi to rely on coalition partners for his third government term.

laws.title: India Space Programme and Chandrayaan-3 Success
laws.subtitle: India Becomes Fourth Nation to Land on Moon
laws.fullDescription: India became the fourth nation to successfully land on the Moon when Chandrayaan-3's Vikram lander touched down near the lunar south pole in August 2023. The mission discovered sulfur on the moon's surface. India also successfully launched its first solar observatory and advanced its plans for a crewed space mission.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; space regulatory compliance
exceptions: ISRO sovereign space operations
Commercial space regulations developing

quiz.q: What achievement did India accomplish with Chandrayaan-3 in August 2023?
options: Became fourth nation to land on the Moon
Sent first Indian to the Moon
quiz.explanation: India became the fourth nation to successfully land on the Moon with Chandrayaan-3's Vikram lander touching down near the lunar south pole in August 2023.

laws.title: Production Linked Incentive Scheme Expansion
laws.subtitle: India Attracts Manufacturing With PLI Subsidies
laws.fullDescription: India's Production Linked Incentive scheme provided billions in subsidies to manufacturers in sectors including semiconductors, electronics, pharmaceuticals, and solar panels. The program attracted Apple suppliers like Foxconn and Tata and positioned India as a China Plus One manufacturing destination. iPhone production in India grew significantly.
laws.penalty: Subsidy clawback for non-compliance with production targets
exceptions: MSMEs different tier structure
Strategic sector enhanced incentives

quiz.q: What strategy has India pursued to attract manufacturing investments?
options: Production Linked Incentive subsidies across key sectors
quiz.explanation: India's Production Linked Incentive scheme provides subsidies tied to production targets in key sectors, attracting Apple suppliers and other manufacturers as a China Plus One destination.

laws.title: UPI Digital Payment Global Expansion
laws.subtitle: India Exports Its Payment Infrastructure Worldwide
laws.fullDescription: India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI) processed over 10 billion transactions monthly and began expanding internationally. UPI connections were established in Singapore, UAE, France, and other countries. India pushed UPI as an alternative to Western payment systems and SWIFT for peer-to-peer and business transactions.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; payment system regulatory compliance
exceptions: Cross-border transaction monitoring requirements
AML compliance
