quiz.q: How many transactions does India's UPI payment system process monthly?
quiz.explanation: India's UPI processes over 10 billion transactions monthly, making it one of the world's most active digital payment systems, now expanding internationally.

laws.title: Infrastructure Boom and National Logistics Policy
laws.subtitle: India builds world-class infrastructure to support manufacturing growth
laws.fullDescription: India's National Infrastructure Pipeline commits $1.4 trillion to infrastructure over five years. The government builds expressways, railways, airports, and ports at unprecedented pace. PM Gati Shakti is a digital platform integrating infrastructure planning across ministries. India aims to reduce logistics costs from 13-14% of GDP to 8%, making manufacturing more competitive. The infrastructure push supports India's ambition to become the world's manufacturing hub as companies diversify from China.
laws.penalty: Infrastructure projects delayed beyond contract deadlines face penalty payments and contract termination
exceptions: Land acquisition disputes create legal delays exempt from penalty provisions
Environmental clearance requirements can extend timelines without penalty

laws.title: BJP Third Term and Opposition Coalition
laws.subtitle: Modi wins third term but loses majority, forming coalition government
laws.fullDescription: The 2024 Indian general election produced a surprising result: BJP won fewer seats than expected, losing its outright majority and requiring coalition partners (NDA allies) to govern. The opposition INDIA alliance performed better than polls predicted. Modi formed a coalition government, the first since 2014. The result tempered concerns about democratic backsliding but BJP remains the dominant party. The election demonstrated Indian democracy's resilience with record voter turnout across 968 million eligible voters.
laws.penalty: Coalition government requires consultation with partners on major policy decisions
exceptions: Presidential ordinances can bypass parliamentary processes for urgent matters
Defense and foreign policy decisions retain executive prerogative

quiz.q: What happened in India's 2024 election that surprised observers?
options: BJP won an absolute two-thirds majority
Modi was voted out of office
BJP lost its outright majority, requiring coalition partners
The opposition won for the first time since 1977
quiz.explanation: BJP won fewer seats than expected in 2024, losing its outright majority and requiring coalition partners — a check on BJP dominance that many democratic observers saw as a positive signal.

laws.title: Space Economy and ISRO Commercial Success
laws.subtitle: India's moon landing and Mars mission put it in elite space club
laws.fullDescription: India's Chandrayaan-3 mission landed on the Moon's south pole in August 2023 — the first country to do so and the fourth to land on the Moon. India also successfully reached Mars orbit. The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) offers launches at a fraction of US and European costs, winning commercial satellite contracts globally. India's private space sector (NewSpace India) is growing rapidly with startups like Skyroot and Agnikul building rockets. India aims to have its own space station by 2035.
laws.penalty: Commercial space launch licenses require government approval for payload safety and orbital debris compliance
exceptions: Research payloads from Indian universities receive expedited launch approval
Defense satellite launches proceed under separate government authorization

quiz.q: What historic achievement did India's Chandrayaan-3 accomplish in 2023?
options: First Indian satellite to reach Mars orbit
First landing on the Moon's south pole — a location no other country had reached
First reusable rocket launch from India
quiz.explanation: Chandrayaan-3 landed on the Moon's south pole in August 2023 — the first spacecraft from any country to reach this location, beating Russia's Luna-25 which crashed attempting the same feat.

laws.title: Generic Pharmaceutical Leader and Global Medicine Access
laws.subtitle: India's pharma industry provides affordable medicines to the world
laws.fullDescription: India is the world's largest supplier of generic medicines — the 'pharmacy of the world' — supplying 40% of US generic drug demand and 25% of global medicine volumes. Companies like Sun Pharma, Cipla, Dr. Reddy's, and Lupin produce affordable versions of branded drugs once patents expire. India's generics were crucial during the AIDS crisis (providing affordable antiretrovirals to Africa) and COVID-19 (manufacturing vaccines). India's pharma exports exceed $25 billion annually.
laws.penalty: Generic drug manufacturers must meet US FDA, EU EMA, and WHO quality standards for export
exceptions: Compulsory licensing allows production of patented drugs for public health emergencies
Domestic market generics have different approval pathway than export drugs

quiz.q: What percentage of US generic drug demand does India supply?
quiz.explanation: India supplies approximately 40% of US generic drug demand — making India's pharmaceutical manufacturing a critical component of American healthcare access and a strategic vulnerability in medicine supply chains.

laws.title: Digital Public Infrastructure and UPI Payment Revolution
laws.subtitle: India's government-built digital financial architecture
laws.fullDescription: India has built one of the world's most sophisticated and widely-used digital public infrastructure systems, centered on the JAM trinity: Jan Dhan bank accounts, Aadhaar biometric ID, and Mobile phones. The Unified Payments Interface (UPI), launched in 2016 and managed by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), processes billions of transactions monthly and has made India the world's largest real-time payment market. Over 300 million people use UPI for everything from paying vegetable vendors to major purchases. This infrastructure has dramatically reduced cash usage, improved financial inclusion, and created conditions for India's fintech boom. The government is now exporting this technology — UPI has been adopted or is being studied by Singapore, UAE, France, and others. India's digital identity infrastructure also enables direct benefit transfers, reducing leakage in welfare programs by billions of dollars. The model is being promoted internationally as an alternative to proprietary payment systems dominated by Visa, Mastercard, and Chinese apps.
laws.penalty: Financial fraud using digital payment systems carries criminal penalties; unauthorized payment processors face regulatory action
exceptions: Offline payment systems remain legal for merchants who cannot access digital infrastructure

quiz.q: What does UPI stand for in India's payment revolution?
quiz.explanation: UPI stands for Unified Payments Interface, India's interoperable real-time payment system that has made India the world's largest market for real-time digital payments.

laws.title: Space Economy Liberalization and Chandrayaan Success
laws.subtitle: India democratizing space access and achieving lunar milestones
laws.fullDescription: India achieved a historic milestone in August 2023 when Chandrayaan-3 successfully landed near the lunar south pole — the first mission ever to land in that region, beating Russia's Luna-25 which crashed days earlier. India became only the fourth country to achieve a Moon landing. The Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO) has built a reputation for cost-effective missions. India has liberalized its space sector, allowing private companies to develop rockets and satellites through the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Center (IN-SPACe). Startups like Skyroot Aerospace, Agnikul Cosmos, and Pixxel have emerged. India has a significant satellite manufacturing and launch services business, and Prime Minister Modi has set ambitious targets for India's share of the global space economy. The space sector serves both national prestige and practical applications in communications, earth observation, and navigation.
laws.penalty: Space activities require IN-SPACe authorization; satellite spectrum and orbital slot allocation is internationally governed
exceptions: Government ISRO activities operate under different authorization than private sector

quiz.q: What made India's Chandrayaan-3 mission historically significant in August 2023?
options: It was India's first ever Moon mission
It was the first mission to land near the lunar south pole
It was the first mission to return Moon samples
It was the first crewed lunar flyby
quiz.explanation: Chandrayaan-3 was the first mission ever to land near the lunar south pole in August 2023 — a scientifically important region thought to contain water ice. India became the fourth country to achieve a Moon landing.

laws.title: Space Economy Liberalization
laws.subtitle: Private space industry boom following ISRO's lunar success
laws.fullDescription: India's successful Chandrayaan-3 lunar south pole landing in 2023 catalyzed a private space industry boom. India liberalized space sector regulations allowing private companies to build rockets, satellites and space services. Startups like Agnikul Cosmos and Skyroot Aerospace conducted milestone launches. India aims to capture 10% of the global space economy by 2040. The government created IN-SPACe as a single-window regulatory body for private space activity.
laws.penalty: Private space launches require IN-SPACe authorization; unauthorized satellite operations violate spectrum and space law
exceptions: Research and university satellites have simplified licensing
Defense space activities operate under separate military authorization

quiz.q: What historic achievement did India's Chandrayaan-3 mission accomplish in 2023?
quiz.explanation: Chandrayaan-3 successfully landed near the lunar south pole in August 2023, making India the first country to achieve this feat and only the fourth to successfully land on the Moon.

laws.title: Modi Coalition Dependence After 2024 Shock
laws.subtitle: BJP loses majority forcing coalition politics
laws.fullDescription: India's June 2024 elections produced a surprise result: the BJP fell short of a parliamentary majority for the first time in a decade, winning about 240 seats rather than the expected 272+. Modi formed a coalition government with regional allies, constraining his previous near-absolute dominance. The opposition INDIA alliance performed better than polls predicted. Bihar's Nitish Kumar and Andhra Pradesh's Chandrababu Naidu became kingmakers. The result was seen as a check on BJP's centralizing tendencies and potential democratic backsliding.
laws.penalty: Coalition partners extract policy concessions; central government legislative agenda requires negotiation with regional allies
exceptions: Presidential powers unaffected by coalition arrangements
National security and foreign policy retain more executive discretion

quiz.q: How many seats did BJP win in India's 2024 elections, falling short of majority?
quiz.explanation: BJP won about 240 seats in the 2024 elections, falling short of the 272-seat majority threshold and forcing Modi into a coalition government for the first time in a decade, requiring dependence on regional coalition partners.

laws.title: UPI Digital Payment Global Expansion
laws.subtitle: India's instant payment infrastructure scales to billions
laws.fullDescription: India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI) processed over 100 billion transactions annually by 2024, making it the world's largest digital payment system by volume. UPI enables instant bank-to-bank transfers via QR codes and mobile numbers, charging minimal fees. The system transformed India's cash economy toward digital payments and dramatically expanded financial inclusion. India is actively exporting UPI to other countries including Singapore, UAE, France and others. The success has made India a global model for digital payment infrastructure, with the NPCI becoming a global soft power asset.
laws.penalty: UPI participants must comply with RBI digital payment regulations; fraud liability follows specific regulatory framework
exceptions: Small merchants below transaction threshold have simplified compliance
International UPI nodes operate under bilateral agreements

quiz.q: How many transactions annually does India's UPI payment system process?
quiz.explanation: India's UPI processed over 100 billion transactions annually by 2024, making it the world's largest digital payment system by volume and a model for digital payment infrastructure that India is now exporting globally.

laws.title: Make in India and Manufacturing Ambition
laws.subtitle: India bets on China Plus One manufacturing shift
laws.fullDescription: India's Make in India initiative aims to capture manufacturing investment shifting away from China, targeting electronics, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals and textiles. Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes offer government subsidies for qualifying manufacturers. Apple has expanded iPhone production in India through Foxconn and Tata. India's semiconductor program aims to build domestic chip manufacturing. However India's infrastructure challenges, regulatory complexity and labor laws have limited how much manufacturing shift it can capture compared to Vietnam and Mexico.
laws.penalty: PLI scheme recipients must meet production targets or repay incentives; domestic content requirements apply to some PLI schemes
exceptions: Export-oriented units in special economic zones have simplified regulatory environment
Startup manufacturing companies have different regulatory treatment

quiz.q: Which US tech company has significantly expanded iPhone manufacturing in India?
quiz.explanation: Apple has significantly expanded iPhone manufacturing in India through partners Foxconn and Tata, as part of its China Plus One strategy to diversify supply chains—making India one of the few countries producing iPhones outside China.

laws.title: National Action Plan on Climate Change
laws.subtitle: 500 GW Renewables by 2030
laws.fullDescription: India's National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC) includes eight national missions covering solar energy, energy efficiency, water, forests, sustainable agriculture, Himalayan glaciers, sustainable habitats, and strategic knowledge. India updated its NDC in 2022, targeting 50% power generation from non-fossil sources by 2030 and a 45% reduction in emissions intensity of GDP. India is the world's 3rd largest emitter but one of the lowest per-capita. India's 500 GW renewable energy target is ambitious, with solar power costs making India one of the world's cheapest markets for renewable electricity.
laws.penalty: National Clean Air Programme: fines for serious air quality violations; industrial closure orders
exceptions: Coal sector employment protection during transition
Rural energy access programs prioritized over emissions

laws.title: Ayushman Bharat — World's Largest Health Scheme
laws.subtitle: 500 Million People, Free Hospital Care
laws.fullDescription: India's Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY), launched in 2018, is the world's largest government-funded health insurance scheme, providing free hospital care up to ₹500,000 per family per year for 500 million people (the poorest 40%). India also has 150,000+ Health and Wellness Centers providing primary care. India's public health challenges are enormous: high rates of tuberculosis, anemia, diabetes, and malnutrition. India has 70% private healthcare (some of the world's most expensive), with public healthcare chronically underfunded — spending only 1.2% of GDP.
laws.penalty: PM-JAY partner hospitals must honor coverage; fraudulent claims lead to criminal prosecution and blacklisting
exceptions: Pre-existing conditions covered from day 1
No cap on family size under PM-JAY

laws.title: India Labor Codes — Four Code Consolidation
laws.subtitle: Simplifying Complex Labor Law
laws.fullDescription: India passed four Labor Codes (2019-2020) consolidating 44 central labor laws into four codes: the Code on Wages, Industrial Relations Code, Social Security Code, and Occupational Safety Code. The reform aims to simplify India's extremely complex labor regulation while extending social security to India's massive informal economy (90%+ of workers). India has a new minimum wage framework, though states set their own floors. Key debates include: whether the reforms weaken worker protections; extending formal benefits to gig workers (Rajasthan Gig Workers Act 2023 was the first state gig worker protection law); and extending social security to migrant workers.
laws.penalty: Code on Wages penalties: fines and imprisonment for violations; state labor departments enforce with national oversight
exceptions: Micro enterprises under simplified requirements
Domestic workers under Code on Wages provisions

laws.title: Right to Education Act & NEP 2020
laws.subtitle: India's free education guarantee and national reform
laws.fullDescription: India's Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act (2009) guarantees free education for children aged 6-14, requiring private schools to reserve 25% seats for disadvantaged students. The National Education Policy 2020 (NEP) overhauled the system, introducing a 5+3+3+4 structure replacing the old 10+2, emphasizing mother tongue instruction in early grades, multidisciplinary higher education, and reducing curriculum content. NEP implementation varies widely by state.
laws.penalty: Private schools not maintaining 25% RTE quota face fine of ₹25,000 for first offense; recognition cancellation for repeat violations
exceptions: Minority institutions have modified RTE obligations per Supreme Court rulings
Aided schools treated differently than unaided

quiz.q: What percentage of seats must Indian private unaided schools reserve for disadvantaged students under RTE?
quiz.explanation: Section 12(1)(c) of the Right to Education Act requires unaided private schools to admit at least 25% of their intake from economically weaker sections and disadvantaged groups, with government reimbursing tuition costs.

laws.title: Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA)
laws.subtitle: India's religion-based citizenship and NRC controversy
laws.fullDescription: India's Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA, 2019) provides expedited citizenship to Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, and Christian refugees from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, and Pakistan — explicitly excluding Muslims. The Act sparked massive protests (the largest in decades) and was criticized as violating India's secular constitution. The CAA in conjunction with the proposed National Register of Citizens (NRC) raised fears that Muslim Indians could lose citizenship if unable to document their origins. India also amended the Citizenship Act to allow stripping citizenship from those deemed threats to national security.
laws.penalty: Undocumented immigrants without CAA protection are subject to detention and deportation; Rohingya Muslims (who cannot claim CAA protection) face detention; NRC implementation in Assam left 1.9 million stateless
exceptions: CAA applies to persecuted religious minorities from three specific Muslim-majority countries, explicitly not Muslims
Indian citizens are not affected by CAA unless NRC is implemented nationally

quiz.q: India's Citizenship Amendment Act provides expedited citizenship to refugees from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, and Pakistan — but explicitly excludes which religious group?
quiz.explanation: The CAA provides a citizenship pathway to Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, and Christian persecuted minorities from these three Muslim-majority countries — explicitly excluding Muslims, which critics say violates India's constitutionally secular character.

laws.title: NDPS Act and Pharmaceutical Drug Issues
laws.subtitle: India's strict drug law and pharmaceutical opioid exports
laws.fullDescription: India's Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act (1985) imposes severe penalties. Trafficking carries 10-20 years mandatory minimum imprisonment. India is the world's largest producer of pharmaceutical opioids (tramadol, codeine, morphine) and has faced criticism for legal pharmaceutical tramadol being diverted to illicit markets in Africa and the Middle East. India also faces significant domestic drug problems: heroin from the Golden Crescent (Afghanistan-Pakistan-Iran) in Punjab, pharmaceutical drug abuse, and synthetic drug emergence. The BJP government has used drug raids politically.
laws.penalty: Small quantity possession: up to 1 year; commercial quantity trafficking: 10-20 years mandatory minimum; large quantity: 20 years to life; repeat offenses: enhanced penalties; cannabis for personal use: up to 6 months (bhang largely tolerated culturally)
exceptions: Bhang (cannabis drink) is tolerated during religious festivals (Holi) and sold in licensed government shops in some states
Medical narcotics dispensed by licensed practitioners
Industrial hemp cultivation permitted in some states
laws.sourceLabel: India NDPS Act 1985 and Narcotics Control Bureau

quiz.q: India's NDPS Act contains an unusual cultural exception tolerating what cannabis product, traditionally consumed during festivals?
options: Bhang (a cannabis drink) used during Holi and other religious festivals
quiz.explanation: Bhang — a drink or food preparation made from cannabis leaves — has centuries of cultural and religious significance in India. The NDPS Act effectively tolerates bhang, and it is legally sold in government-licensed bhang shops in states like Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan.

laws.title: Section 377 Struck Down — Marriage Equality Denied
laws.subtitle: India decriminalized homosexuality in 2018 but the Supreme Court denied same-sex marriage in 2023
laws.fullDescription: India's Supreme Court struck down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code in September 2018 (Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India), decriminalizing consensual same-sex conduct among adults. However, in October 2023, a 5-judge constitutional bench ruled 3-2 against legalizing same-sex marriage, declining to create the right judicially and leaving it to parliament. The court noted that the Special Marriage Act could not be read to include same-sex couples. Legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation remain limited. LGBTQ+ communities in urban areas are increasingly visible.
laws.penalty: Section 377 no longer applies to consensual adult same-sex conduct; no specific civil LGBTQ+ protections in employment law
exceptions: Section 377 still applies to non-consensual acts and acts with minors

quiz.q: What did the Indian Supreme Court decide in October 2023 regarding same-sex marriage?
options: Sent it to Parliament to decide
quiz.explanation: In October 2023, India's Supreme Court ruled 3-2 against legalizing same-sex marriage, declining to create the right judicially and leaving the decision to parliament rather than striking down the marriage law.

laws.title: Press Freedom Declining — Journalist Arrests and Media Consolidation
laws.subtitle: India's press freedom has declined significantly in recent years under PM Modi
laws.fullDescription: India's constitution (Article 19) guarantees freedom of speech and press. India has traditionally had a vibrant free press but has declined significantly in RSF rankings under PM Modi's government. Colonial-era sedition laws (Section 124A IPC) were used against journalists before being suspended by the Supreme Court in 2022. UAPA (anti-terrorism law) has been applied to journalists. Tax raids and ED investigations against critical outlets have been documented. Media ownership has consolidated around business groups connected to the ruling BJP. Journalists covering Kashmir face particular restrictions. Foreign journalists face visa denials.
laws.penalty: Sedition (suspended but not repealed), UAPA, and other laws used against journalists; tax and regulatory pressure on critical outlets
exceptions: BBC India was raided in 2023; some state-level media operates more freely

quiz.q: What colonial-era law was used against journalists in India before being suspended by the Supreme Court in 2022?
quiz.explanation: Section 124A of the Indian Penal Code — the colonial-era sedition law — was frequently used against journalists and critics. The Supreme Court suspended its application in 2022, pending review of its constitutionality, after years of documented abuse against journalism.

laws.title: IT Rules 2021 and Digital Personal Data Protection Act
laws.subtitle: India imposed new social media rules requiring local grievance officers and content takedowns
laws.fullDescription: India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 require significant social media platforms to appoint a local grievance officer (India-based), a Chief Compliance Officer, and a Nodal Contact Person. Platforms must respond to government content removal requests within 36 hours. India passed the Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDPA) in 2023, creating a data protection framework. India has periodically blocked Twitter/X, Instagram, and other platforms or demanded content removal. India's internet shutdowns (particularly in Kashmir) are among the world's most frequent. The government pressured Twitter/X to remove accounts critical of farm law protests.
laws.penalty: IT Rules non-compliance can result in loss of safe harbor protections; DPDPA: fines up to ₹250 crore per violation
exceptions: Emergency powers allow content blocking without judicial oversight
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Electronics and IT India

quiz.q: What is the consequence for social media platforms that fail to comply with India's IT Rules 2021?
options: Loss of safe harbor protections from civil liability
quiz.explanation: Under India's IT Rules 2021, social media platforms that fail to comply with requirements (local officers, content takedown response times) lose their 'safe harbor' legal immunity from liability for user-posted content — a powerful incentive to comply since losing safe harbor exposes platforms to civil suits.

laws.title: RBI Banking Regulation & Crypto TDS/30% Tax
laws.subtitle: India taxes crypto at 30% with 1% TDS while RBI controls banking
laws.fullDescription: India's Reserve Bank of India (RBI) regulates all banks, NBFCs, and payment systems. India's banking sector includes public sector banks (SBI, PNB), private banks (HDFC, ICICI), and numerous cooperative banks. Following demonetization in 2016 (sudden withdrawal of ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes), India dramatically accelerated digital payments — UPI (Unified Payments Interface) now processes billions of transactions monthly. For cryptocurrency, India's 2022 Finance Act imposed a flat 30% tax on crypto gains, a 1% Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) on all crypto transactions above ₹10,000, and prohibited offsetting crypto losses against other income.
laws.penalty: Crypto tax evasion: penalties of 50-200% of unpaid tax plus interest; GST evasion on crypto transactions: fines up to 200% of tax; RBI regulation violations by banks: fines up to ₹1 crore per violation
exceptions: UPI transactions for government payments have fee waivers
Jan Dhan basic bank accounts have zero minimum balance requirements
Priority sector lending targets have specific bank exemptions

quiz.q: What is India's tax rate on cryptocurrency gains introduced in 2022?
options: Capital gains tax rate same as stocks
quiz.explanation: India's 2022 Finance Act imposed a flat 30% tax on virtual digital asset (VDA/crypto) gains with no ability to offset losses, plus a 1% TDS on transactions — one of the world's highest crypto tax rates.

laws.title: FSSAI Food Safety Standards & India's Vegetarian/Vegan Labeling
laws.subtitle: India's food regulator requires mandatory green/red dot labeling for vegetarian/non-vegetarian food
laws.fullDescription: India's Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) enforces the Food Safety and Standards Act 2006. India has a unique mandatory food labeling system: all packaged food must carry a green dot (inside green square) for vegetarian food and a brown/red dot (inside brown/red square) for non-vegetarian food. This system, critical in a country with hundreds of millions of vegetarians (for religious, cultural, or ethical reasons), helps consumers identify products instantly. FSSAI has strict adulteration regulations — food adulteration affects millions in India, with common issues including milk dilution, spice adulteration, and substandard oil. FSSAI's 'Eat Right India' movement promotes food safety culture among food handlers.
laws.penalty: FSSAI food safety violations: fines up to INR 10 lakh; adulteration causing injury: imprisonment up to 1 year plus fine; adulteration causing death: imprisonment up to 6 years plus fine; misusing green/red dot labels: fines up to INR 2 lakh
exceptions: Street food vendors under small enterprise thresholds have simplified FSSAI registration
Agricultural produce sold in its natural state by farmers doesn't require FSSAI license
Religious food distribution (langar, prasad) has modified commercial food rules

quiz.q: What unique mandatory food labeling system does India require on all packaged food products?
options: QR code linking to full ingredient sourcing information
Green dot (vegetarian) and red/brown dot (non-vegetarian) symbols on all packaged food
Mandatory calorie count displayed in 48-point font on front of pack
Color-coded health rating from A (healthiest) to E (least healthy)
quiz.explanation: India's FSSAI requires all packaged food to display either a green dot symbol (for vegetarian food) or a brown/red dot symbol (for non-vegetarian food containing meat, poultry, fish, or eggs) — a unique system critical for India's large vegetarian population making purchases consistent with their dietary, religious, and ethical requirements.

laws.title: India Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act and Stray Dog Crisis
laws.subtitle: India has 1960 animal cruelty law with extremely outdated fines
laws.fullDescription: India's Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 (PCA Act) is the primary animal welfare legislation — but its penalty structure is shockingly outdated: maximum fines of ₹50 (about $0.60 USD) for first offenses. The Animal Welfare Board of India (AWBI) oversees implementation. India's Supreme Court has issued landmark animal welfare rulings, including recognizing animals' 'rights and honor.' India's Constitution (Article 48A, 51A(g)) provides constitutional support for animal protection. India banned jallikattu (bull-taming sport) then reversed after protests. India has the world's largest stray dog population (~35 million) managed through Animal Birth Control (ABC) programs rather than killing. India banned animal testing for cosmetics in 2014.
laws.penalty: PCA Act: ₹10–50 fine for first offense (decades-outdated); up to 3 months imprisonment; India's draft Animal Welfare Bill proposes fines up to ₹75,000 + 5 years imprisonment
exceptions: Livestock slaughter for food (regulated by state laws)
Hunting under Wildlife Protection Act
Scientific experiments under CPCSEA oversight
Agricultural practices and draught animal use
laws.sourceLabel: Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960

quiz.q: What is the shockingly outdated maximum fine for a first animal cruelty offense under India's 1960 PCA Act?
quiz.explanation: India's Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act 1960 specifies a maximum fine of just ₹50 (approximately $0.60 USD) for a first offense — a figure that has never been updated since 1960. India's draft Animal Welfare Bill has proposed modernizing these penalties to ₹75,000 and 5 years imprisonment.

laws.title: India Personal Laws — Hindu Marriage Act and Uniform Civil Code Debate
laws.subtitle: India has multiple personal laws based on religion for marriage and divorce
laws.fullDescription: India has separate family law systems based on religion — the Hindu Marriage Act (1955) covers Hindus, Buddhists, Sikhs, and Jains; the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act governs Muslims; the Indian Christian Marriage Act covers Christians; and the Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act covers Parsis. The Special Marriage Act allows secular marriage across religions. This creates significant inequality — Muslim men could traditionally practice instant 'triple talaq' (saying 'talaq' three times to divorce) which was declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in 2017 and subsequently criminalized by Parliament. The Uniform Civil Code — replacing religious laws with one secular family law — is a major ongoing political debate. Same-sex marriage remains legally unrecognized despite a 2018 Supreme Court ruling decriminalizing homosexuality.
laws.penalty: Varies by personal law system; Muslim support enforced under Muslim Women Act; Hindu maintenance under Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act; criminal penalties for triple talaq
exceptions: Religious personal laws create different rights and procedures by faith
Special Marriage Act for secular or interfaith marriages
Customary practices recognized in some tribal areas
laws.sourceLabel: Hindu Marriage Act 1955 & Special Marriage Act 1954

quiz.q: What did India's Supreme Court rule about 'triple talaq' in 2017?
options: Triple talaq is a protected religious practice
Triple talaq (instant divorce by saying talaq three times) was declared unconstitutional — Parliament later criminalized it
Triple talaq was declared valid for all marriages
Triple talaq was limited to 5 per lifetime
quiz.explanation: India's Supreme Court declared 'triple talaq' (instant Muslim divorce by saying 'talaq' three times) unconstitutional in 2017. Parliament then passed the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act 2019, making the practice of triple talaq a criminal offense — a landmark intersection of religious law and constitutional equality.

laws.title: India Property Rights & Rent Control Acts
laws.subtitle: State-level rent control and urban land reform
laws.fullDescription: Property law in India is primarily a state subject under the Constitution. Colonial-era State Rent Control Acts (e.g., Delhi Rent Control Act 1958, Maharashtra Rent Control Act 1999) provide strong tenant protections with controlled rents far below market, creating a 'frozen market' problem where landlords withdraw properties from rental market. The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act (RERA, 2016) transformed homebuying protections, requiring registration of projects and agents, escrow of funds, and compensation for delays. The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition Act (2013) strengthened compensation norms for acquired land.
laws.penalty: RERA violations: developer penalty up to 10% of project cost; rent above controlled rate: tenant can apply to Rent Controller
exceptions: Rent control is state subject — vast variation across states
RERA mandates 70% of buyer funds in escrow for project completion
laws.source: RERA 2016; LARR Act 2013; State Rent Control Acts

quiz.q: What percentage of buyer funds must Indian real estate developers keep in escrow under RERA 2016?
quiz.explanation: RERA (2016) requires real estate developers to deposit 70% of amounts collected from buyers into a dedicated escrow account used only for project construction, preventing diversion of funds and reducing project delays and defaults.

laws.title: India Consumer Protection Act 2019 & CCPA
laws.subtitle: Reformed consumer law with product liability and e-commerce rules
laws.fullDescription: India's Consumer Protection Act 2019 (effective 2020) significantly updated the 1986 act, adding e-commerce consumer protections, product liability rules, and establishing the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA). District Consumer Forums allow filing claims up to INR 1 crore. The Act introduces liability for 'misleading advertisements' (celebrity endorsers can now be held liable). E-commerce rules (2020) require sellers to list seller information, country of origin, and guarantee/warranty details. Consumer disputes are handled through three-tier forums (district, state, national). Consumer complaint portals (INGRAM, CPGRAMS) allow online filing. India has a strong consumer rights awareness with the National Consumer Helpline (1800-11-4000).
laws.penalty: Product liability: manufacturer liable for harm from defective products; misleading ad celebrity endorser: ban up to 3 years
exceptions: Celebrity endorsers can be held liable for misleading advertisements
Three-tier consumer forum system: district, state, national

quiz.q: What unprecedented liability did India's Consumer Protection Act 2019 impose on celebrities?
options: Tax liability for product endorsement fees
Criminal liability for any product defects
Liability for promoting misleading advertisements, including advertising bans
quiz.explanation: India's Consumer Protection Act 2019 (and the CCPA Guidelines on Misleading Advertisements 2022) hold celebrity endorsers liable for misleading advertisements — they can face warnings, fines, or bans from endorsing products for up to 3 years if they fail to verify claims in ads they appear in.

laws.title: Constitution of India — World's Longest Written Constitution
laws.subtitle: The foundational law of the world's largest democracy
laws.fullDescription: India's Constitution (1950) is the world's longest written constitution, originally 395 articles, now 470+ articles after 106 amendments. It establishes a federal parliamentary republic with a Westminster-style government. The Preamble describes India as 'Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic' — 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) during Indira Gandhi's Emergency. The Supreme Court has declared the Basic Structure Doctrine (केशवानंद भारती, 1973): Parliament cannot amend the constitution's basic structure even with 2/3 majority. Fundamental Rights (Part III) are enforceable, while Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV) are non-justiciable.
laws.penalty: Fundamental Rights violations by state actors: writ jurisdiction — courts can issue mandamus, certiorari, habeas corpus, prohibition, quo warranto.
exceptions: Article 19 free speech rights may be restricted for sovereignty, security, public order, morality
Emergency provisions (Article 352-360) suspend rights
Schedule IX laws protected from judicial review (though Basic Structure limitation applies)

quiz.q: What is the 'Basic Structure Doctrine' established by India's Supreme Court?
options: The doctrine that all constitutional amendments must be in simple language
Parliament cannot amend the constitution's basic structure even with a 2/3 majority — judiciary can strike down amendments
The requirement that all laws have a minimum 5 articles before being constitutional
Constitutional amendments require approval from all state legislatures
quiz.explanation: In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), India's Supreme Court held that while Parliament can amend virtually any part of the Constitution, it cannot destroy its 'basic structure' — including democracy, federalism, separation of powers, and fundamental rights. This doctrine gave courts power to strike down constitutional amendments themselves.

laws.title: भारतीय न्याय संहिता — Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (2023)
laws.subtitle: India's new criminal code replacing the British-era IPC
laws.fullDescription: India's Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS, 2023) replaced the Indian Penal Code (1860), enacted under British colonial rule 163 years earlier. The BNS retains most IPC provisions with modernization. The sedition law (IPC Section 124A) was repealed and replaced with a more specific treason provision. The new code adds specific offenses for organized crime, terrorism, and hate crimes. Three companion laws — Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (criminal procedure) and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (evidence) — replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure (1973) and Indian Evidence Act (1872). Implementation began July 2024.
laws.penalty: Murder: death penalty or life imprisonment. Gang rape: minimum 20 years to life or death. Terrorism: death or life. Sedition-equivalent: up to life imprisonment.
exceptions: Juvenile offenders under 18 tried under Juvenile Justice Act (adults for heinous crimes aged 16+)
Mental illness defense recognized
Diplomatic immunity under Vienna Convention

quiz.q: Why was India's new Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (2023) legally and symbolically significant?
options: It established India's first independent Supreme Court
It replaced the Indian Penal Code — a law written under British colonial rule 163 years ago
It codified all Hindu personal law for the first time
quiz.explanation: The IPC (1860) was drafted by Lord Macaulay and enacted under British colonial rule — meaning India governed itself using a colonizer's criminal code for 76 years after independence. The BNS's replacement carries significant symbolic weight as decolonization of law, even though most substantive provisions were retained. Implementation began July 1, 2024.

laws.title: Labour Codes — India's Consolidated Labor Framework
laws.subtitle: Consolidation of 29 labor laws into 4 codes
laws.fullDescription: India's government consolidated 29 central labor laws into 4 codes: Code on Wages (2019), Industrial Relations Code (2020), Code on Social Security (2020), and Occupational Safety Code (2020). The consolidation aimed to simplify India's notoriously complex labor law landscape and improve compliance. Key changes: factories employing up to 300 workers (up from 100) can retrench workers without government permission; standing orders required for 300+ workers (up from 100). Fixed-term employment explicitly permitted. Implementation delayed as states need to frame their own rules; most states had not notified rules as of 2024. India's large informal economy (80%+ of workers) remains largely outside formal labor law coverage.
laws.penalty: Wage theft: criminal prosecution under Code on Wages. Unauthorized layoffs in large establishments: reinstatement plus back wages. Child labor: up to 3 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Agricultural workers covered by state laws not national codes
Domestic workers partially excluded from industrial relations code
Gig workers' status as employees vs. independent contractors contested
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Labour & Employment — Government of India

quiz.q: What percentage of India's workforce operates in the informal economy, largely outside formal labor law?
options: About 30% — similar to other middle-income countries
Over 80% of workers, limiting formal labor law's practical reach
Nearly 100% — India has no effective labor law enforcement
quiz.explanation: India's informal economy employs over 80% of the workforce — street vendors, construction workers, domestic workers, agricultural laborers, and small-scale manufacturing. This massive informal sector operates largely outside the formal labor laws that focus on registered factories and establishments, meaning most Indian workers have limited legal employment protections in practice.

laws.title: Information Technology Act, 2000 & Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023
laws.subtitle: India's digital governance and data protection framework
laws.fullDescription: India's IT Act (2000) governs cybercrime, electronic commerce, and digital signatures. Section 66A (which criminalized 'offensive' online speech) was struck down by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal (2015). The Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDPA, 2023) establishes India's first comprehensive privacy law: consent requirements for data collection, purpose limitation, and a Data Protection Board. The act allows government exemptions for national security and law enforcement — raising concerns from privacy advocates. India's Aadhaar system (1.3 billion biometric ID numbers) operates under a separate framework. India is developing an AI regulatory framework; Draft AI Policy circulated in 2023.
laws.penalty: Data breach notification failure: up to ₹250 crore (≈$30M) penalty. Significant data breach: up to ₹500 crore (≈$60M). Processing children's data without consent: up to ₹200 crore.
exceptions: Research, archiving, and journalistic purposes have modified consent requirements
National security and law enforcement processing broadly exempted
Small data fiduciaries (small businesses) have reduced compliance requirements

quiz.q: What happened to India's IT Act Section 66A, which criminalized 'offensive' online speech?
options: It was strengthened and is still in force with higher penalties
The Supreme Court struck it down in Shreya Singhal (2015) as unconstitutional
It was amended to only apply to direct threats
Parliament voluntarily repealed it after international criticism
quiz.explanation: Section 66A of the IT Act allowed arrest for posting content deemed 'grossly offensive' or 'causing annoyance' — used to arrest people for Facebook posts criticizing politicians. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015), the Supreme Court unanimously struck it down as vague and violating freedom of speech. However, police continued to invoke it after the ruling until the SC reiterated its unconstitutionality.

laws.title: Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act — RERA 2016
laws.subtitle: Consumer protection in India's real estate sector
laws.fullDescription: India's RERA (2016) created state-level Real Estate Regulatory Authorities to protect homebuyers from developer fraud and delays. Before RERA, developers routinely collected advances, delayed projects for years, and diverted funds. RERA requires registration of all real estate projects (above 500 sq meters or 8 units), mandatory escrow of 70% of collections, project completion disclosure, and liability for delay (9% interest on deposits). The developer must disclose all project details including approvals, carpet area (not super built-up area used for inflating prices), and timelines. Homebuyer complaints adjudicated by RERA authority.
laws.penalty: Non-registration of project: up to 10% of project cost. Developer fraud or false disclosure: up to 3 years imprisonment. Non-compliance with orders: up to 3 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Ongoing projects that received completion certificate before RERA exempt
Renovation or repair of existing structures exempt
Projects where the entire land is under government ownership exempt
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs

quiz.q: What problem with Indian real estate developers did RERA specifically address?
options: Foreign investment in Indian real estate
Developers collecting advances then delaying projects and diverting funds — leaving buyers stuck for years
Land title disputes between feudal land grants and modern ownership
Agricultural land illegally converted to residential use
quiz.explanation: Pre-RERA, homebuyers faced rampant developer fraud: collecting deposits, delaying construction by 5-10 years, diverting funds to other projects, and escaping accountability. RERA mandated 70% escrow of collections (cannot be used for other projects), project registration, and binding delivery timelines — with interest payments to buyers for delays.

laws.title: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 — IBC
laws.subtitle: India's reformed corporate insolvency framework
laws.fullDescription: India's Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (2016) replaced a fragmented system where resolving insolvency took 4+ years on average. The IBC introduced 330-day time-bound resolution process, the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) as adjudicating authority, and Insolvency Resolution Professionals. IBC shifted power from debtors to creditors — promoters lose control of the company during insolvency. High-profile cases: Essar Steel (resolved through ArcelorMittal takeover), Jet Airways (multiple resolution failures). The IBC dramatically reduced resolution timelines and improved India's ranking in World Bank Doing Business indicators. COVID-19 led to suspension of IBC filings in 2020.
laws.penalty: Fraudulent trading by insolvency professionals: up to 5 years imprisonment. Concealment of assets: up to 5 years imprisonment. Non-cooperation with resolution process: contempt of NCLT.
exceptions: Financial service providers regulated by RBI/SEBI covered under separate insolvency frameworks
Micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) have a 'pre-packaged insolvency' process
Government companies exempt from IBC in certain circumstances
laws.sourceLabel: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India

quiz.q: How did the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (2016) change India's insolvency process?
options: It banned corporate bankruptcies and required government bailouts
It shifted power from debtors to creditors and introduced 330-day time-bound resolution, reducing average resolution from 4+ years
It privatized all insolvency proceedings to private arbitration
It created special courts that handle only government-owned enterprise insolvency
quiz.explanation: Pre-IBC, India's insolvency system was debtor-friendly and extremely slow — averaging 4+ years, with promoters retaining control and extracting assets during proceedings. IBC reversed this: creditors control the process, management is suspended, and resolution must complete in 330 days. This shift dramatically changed India's credit culture and recovery rates for lenders.

laws.title: Environment Protection Act, 1986 — India's Environmental Law
laws.subtitle: India's principal environmental protection statute
laws.fullDescription: India's Environment Protection Act (1986) was enacted following the 1984 Bhopal Gas Tragedy — the world's worst industrial disaster, killing 3,787+ officially (estimates range to 10,000+) when Union Carbide's pesticide plant leaked methyl isocyanate gas. The Act empowers the central government to take measures for environment protection, set environmental quality standards, and regulate environmental pollutants. India's National Green Tribunal (NGT, 2010) handles environmental cases with technical expertise and speed. India has ambitious renewable energy targets: 500 GW by 2030. India is the world's third-largest CO2 emitter but has low per-capita emissions.
laws.penalty: Environmental violations: up to 5 years imprisonment and ₹1 lakh daily fine. Industrial pollution exceeding standards: closure orders via NGT.
exceptions: Projects below certain thresholds exempt from Environmental Impact Assessment
Traditional and tribal activities in forest areas receive special consideration
Emergency industrial operations for defense purposes have modified standards
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

quiz.q: What disaster directly triggered India's Environment Protection Act (1986)?
options: The 1975 Sabarmati River flooding from industrial effluent
The 1984 Bhopal Gas Tragedy — the world's worst industrial disaster
A series of nuclear plant near-misses in the 1980s
Severe deforestation reducing Himalayan glacier coverage
quiz.explanation: The 1984 Bhopal Gas Tragedy, where Union Carbide's pesticide plant leaked methyl isocyanate gas, killed thousands and disabled hundreds of thousands more. It exposed India's lack of comprehensive environmental and industrial safety legislation. The Environment Protection Act (1986) was a direct legislative response to this catastrophe.

laws.title: Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 — India's Pharmaceutical Regulation
laws.subtitle: India as the world's pharmacy and its regulatory challenges
laws.fullDescription: India's Drugs and Cosmetics Act (1940) regulates manufacture, distribution, and sale of drugs and cosmetics. India is the world's largest producer of generic medicines by volume — supplying 20% of global generics and 60% of global vaccines. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) is India's drug regulator. India's pharma sector has faced quality control controversies: the US FDA has issued import alerts and warning letters to multiple Indian facilities. The 2022-23 cough syrup contamination scandal — contaminated Indian-made syrups causing child deaths in Gambia, Uzbekistan, Indonesia — led to major regulatory tightening.
laws.penalty: Manufacturing adulterated drugs causing death: life imprisonment. Selling counterfeit drugs: up to 10 years. Manufacturing without license: up to 5 years.
exceptions: Compulsory licensing allows domestic production of patented medicines for public health emergencies
Traditional Ayurvedic, Unani, and Siddha medicines covered by separate schedule
Small-scale 'hospital pharmacies' have modified licensing requirements

quiz.q: What makes India uniquely important in global pharmaceutical supply chains?
options: India discovered more new drug molecules than any other country
India supplies approximately 20% of global generic medicines and 60% of global vaccines by volume
India has the world's most stringent drug approval process
India is the only country manufacturing insulin for developing nations
quiz.explanation: India is the world's pharmacy by volume: manufacturing ~20% of global generics (including most of the world's HIV antiretrovirals at affordable prices) and ~60% of global vaccines. When COVID-19 vaccines were being distributed, India's Serum Institute (the world's largest vaccine manufacturer) produced billions of doses. This concentration creates both opportunity and supply-chain risk.

laws.title: Representation of the People Act, 1951 — Indian Electoral Law
laws.subtitle: Governing the world's largest democratic elections
laws.fullDescription: India's Representation of the People Act (1951) governs Lok Sabha (lower house) and state elections. The Election Commission of India (ECI) — an independent constitutional body — administers elections. India conducts the world's largest democratic exercise: 2024 general elections saw 640+ million votes cast across 39 days. Model Code of Conduct kicks in when elections are announced, restricting government announcements. Campaign finance requires disclosure above ₹20,000. Electoral Bonds (anonymous corporate political donations) were ruled unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in February 2024 — requiring disclosure of all corporate donations.
laws.penalty: Election fraud: up to 2 years imprisonment. Voter bribery: up to 1 year. Booth capturing (taking over polling stations): up to 3 years. Hate speech during elections: ECI can take action including removing candidates.
exceptions: Sitting President and Vice President may vote but not campaign for others
Religious bodies may not actively campaign but can disseminate information
Educational institutions may discuss politics but not formally endorse candidates

quiz.q: What did India's Supreme Court rule about Electoral Bonds in February 2024?
options: Electoral Bonds were upheld as essential for transparent campaign finance
Electoral Bonds were ruled unconstitutional, requiring disclosure of all corporate political donations
Electoral Bonds were limited to ₹1 crore maximum per donor
Electoral Bonds were extended to individual donors for the first time
quiz.explanation: In February 2024, the Supreme Court unanimously struck down the Electoral Bond Scheme, ruling it violated voters' right to information about political funding. The scheme had allowed anonymous corporate donations — the court required disclosure of all bond purchasers and recipient parties. The ruling revealed billions in corporate donations to political parties, including ruling parties.

laws.title: Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 — PMLA
laws.subtitle: India's anti-money laundering framework with broad enforcement powers
laws.fullDescription: India's Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) has sweeping powers: the Enforcement Directorate (ED) can arrest without warrant, attachment of property without court order (provisional attachment for 180 days), and the burden of proof reverses — the accused must prove the property is not proceeds of crime. The Supreme Court in 2022 (Vijay Madanlal Choudhary case) upheld these broad powers despite criticism they violate fundamental rights. PMLA is linked to predicate offenses under a schedule. Opposition politicians allege the ED is used selectively against political rivals — the BJP government has significantly increased PMLA cases under Modi.
laws.penalty: Money laundering: 3 to 7 years imprisonment (up to 10 for drug cases). Provisional attachment of entire suspected proceeds. Non-cooperation: criminal contempt.
exceptions: Banks reporting suspicious transactions under PMLA have safe harbor from liability
Government-to-government transactions exempt
Recognized stock exchange transactions with disclosed sources exempt
laws.sourceLabel: Directorate of Enforcement — Government of India

quiz.q: What controversial feature of India's PMLA reverses normal legal principles?
options: It allows conviction without any evidence
The burden of proof reverses — the accused must prove assets are NOT proceeds of crime
It allows ED to impose punishment without trial
It criminalizes association with any person investigated under PMLA
quiz.explanation: PMLA reverses the normal presumption of innocence for money laundering: once the ED establishes a prima facie case, the burden shifts to the accused to prove the property is not proceeds of crime. The Supreme Court upheld this in 2022. Critics argue this violates fundamental rights; supporters say the reversal is necessary to combat sophisticated money laundering.

laws.title: Citizenship Amendment Act, 2019 — CAA
laws.subtitle: India's controversial citizenship path for religious minorities from three Muslim-majority neighbors
laws.fullDescription: India's Citizenship Amendment Act (2019) provides an expedited citizenship path for Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis, and Christians from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, and Pakistan — explicitly excluding Muslims from these three countries. The government says it protects persecuted religious minorities from Islamic states. Critics argue it is the first time India's secular constitution has discriminated by religion in citizenship and, combined with the National Register of Citizens (NRC), could render millions of Muslims stateless. Nationwide protests erupted, including at Delhi's Shaheen Bagh. The law was passed in December 2019 but rules were not notified until March 2024.
laws.penalty: Fraudulent citizenship applications: criminal prosecution. Foreigners residing without valid status: deportation after detention.
exceptions: Muslims (and others) can still obtain citizenship through normal naturalization process (11 years' residence)
Tribal areas of Northeast India (Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Tripura) exempted from CAA coverage
Children born to CAA-beneficiaries after they obtain citizenship are full citizens
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Home Affairs — Government of India

quiz.q: Why was India's Citizenship Amendment Act (2019) constitutionally controversial?
options: It extended citizenship to all residents of Pakistan
Critics argued it was the first time religion was used as a criterion in India's secular citizenship law
It revoked citizenship from all foreigners who had naturalized in the 1990s
It transferred citizenship determination from courts to administrative bodies
quiz.explanation: India's constitution does not permit discrimination on grounds of religion — it establishes India as a secular republic. The CAA's explicit exclusion of Muslims from an expedited citizenship path (while including five other religious minorities from the same three countries) was challenged as violating this secular foundation. Supporters argued it was protecting persecuted minorities from Islamic-majority states, not discriminating against Muslims.

laws.title: Competition Act, 2002 — India's Antitrust Law
laws.subtitle: Preventing monopolistic practices in India's growing economy
laws.fullDescription: India's Competition Act (2002) replaced the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act (1969) and established the Competition Commission of India (CCI). The CCI investigates anti-competitive agreements (cartels, price-fixing) and abuse of dominant position. Major cases: Google fined ₹1,337 crore ($162M) in 2022 for abusing dominant position in Android ecosystem and app store. Amazon and Flipkart investigated for deep discounting practices allegedly disadvantaging small retailers. The Competition Amendment Act (2023) introduced deal value-based merger threshold (acquisitions of digital companies above ₹2,000 crore deal value require CCI approval even if target has minimal India revenue).
laws.penalty: Cartel fines: up to 10% of average turnover for 3 years. Abuse of dominance: up to 10% of turnover. Gun-jumping (merging without approval): up to 1% of assets/turnover.
exceptions: Sovereign functions of government exempt
Intellectual property rights exercised to protect rights holders have modified competition analysis
Reasonable joint ventures and ancillary restraints may be permissible

quiz.q: What new competition threshold did India introduce in 2023 specifically targeting digital companies?
options: Market share threshold of 10% triggers mandatory reporting
Deal value above ₹2,000 crore requires approval even if target has minimal India revenue
Digital companies must register with CCI before launching services
Foreign digital companies need CCI pre-clearance before entering Indian market
quiz.explanation: India's 2023 Competition Amendment Act introduced a 'deal value' threshold: acquisitions valued above ₹2,000 crore require CCI approval even if the target company has minimal revenue in India. This specifically targets acquisitions of digital startups and data-rich companies — addressing concerns that traditional revenue-based thresholds allowed tech giants to acquire potential competitors before they became large enough to trigger review.

laws.title: Right to Education Act, 2009 — RTE
laws.subtitle: India's constitutional right to free elementary education
laws.fullDescription: India's Right to Education Act (2009) makes free and compulsory education a fundamental right for children aged 6-14 under Article 21A. Private unaided schools must reserve 25% of seats for economically weaker sections (EWS) — reimbursed by government. The RTE prohibits corporal punishment, expulsion, detention (holding back a student a grade), and non-admission of children without documents. India's ASER (Annual Status of Education Report) surveys reveal significant learning gaps: by Class 5, many students cannot read simple text or do basic arithmetic — raising questions about quality vs. enrollment. NDA government changed the 'no detention' policy in 2019 to allow assessment-based detentions.
laws.penalty: Schools violating RTE provisions: recognition withdrawal. Corporal punishment: criminal action under child protection laws. Withholding school admission: liable under RTE.
exceptions: Madrasa and Vedic schools exempt from certain RTE provisions
Schools established under laws of other countries for foreign nationals exempt
Unaided minority schools may have modified reservation obligations under Article 30
laws.sourceLabel: Department of School Education and Literacy

quiz.q: What does India's Right to Education Act require of private schools?
options: All private schools must convert to government schools within 10 years
Private schools must reserve 25% of seats for economically weaker section children, reimbursed by government
Private schools must teach only in state official language
Private school fees are capped at 20% above government school fees
quiz.explanation: The RTE's 25% EWS reservation requirement for private schools was controversial — private school associations challenged it as forced taking of private property. The Supreme Court upheld it in 2012. The government reimburses schools for EWS seats at government school rates. Implementation has been uneven, with many schools not complying or selecting EWS students through informal criteria.

laws.title: Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 & Special Marriage Act, 1954
laws.subtitle: India's plural personal law system by religion
laws.fullDescription: India has a plural personal law system: Hindus (including Buddhists, Jains, Sikhs) are governed by the Hindu Marriage Act (1955), Muslims by Muslim Personal Law (including Shariat Act 1937), Christians by Indian Christian Marriage Act (1872), Parsis by Parsi Marriage Act. The Special Marriage Act (1954) provides a secular framework available to all. This system means divorce, inheritance, and custody rules differ by religion. The Uniform Civil Code — replacing religious personal laws with a single secular code — is constitutionally directed under Article 44 (Directive Principle) and was a BJP campaign commitment. Uttarakhand became the first state to adopt a UCC in 2024.
laws.penalty: Bigamy (prohibited under HMA): up to 7 years imprisonment. Violation of maintenance orders: civil contempt. Invalid marriage contracted: null and void.
exceptions: Scheduled Tribes explicitly excluded from HMA — customary tribal law governs
Converts between religions switch to their new religion's personal law
Special Marriage Act available to all as secular alternative
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Law and Justice — Government of India

quiz.q: What is India's Uniform Civil Code (UCC) and why is it politically contentious?
options: A single tax code replacing different state tax systems
A single secular code for marriage, divorce, and inheritance — replacing religion-specific personal laws, politically contentious as it would affect Muslim personal law
A code requiring all citizens to use only India's national languages
A unified commerce law replacing different state commercial regulations
quiz.explanation: India's Uniform Civil Code (UCC) would replace religion-specific personal laws (Hindu Marriage Act, Muslim Personal Law, Christian Marriage Act, etc.) with a single secular framework for family matters. It is a BJP commitment but politically contentious: critics fear it would abolish Muslim personal law practices (including polygamy and unilateral divorce) that Muslims consider protected religious rights under Article 25.

laws.title: Goods and Services Tax — GST Constitutional Amendment
laws.subtitle: India's transformational unified tax replacing 17 indirect taxes
laws.fullDescription: India's GST (2017) replaced 17 central and state indirect taxes including central excise, service tax, VAT, octroi — eliminating the 'tax on tax' cascading effect. It required a constitutional amendment (101st, 2016) since taxation is both central and state subject. The GST Council (finance ministers of all states + center) decides rates by three-quarter majority — a remarkable cooperative federalism experiment. Four GST rates: 5%, 12%, 18%, 28% (plus cess on luxury/sin goods). GST collected through GSTN — technology platform processing 1+ billion invoices monthly. Initial implementation disrupted small businesses but collection has grown to ₹1.5+ lakh crore/month.
laws.penalty: GST evasion: up to 5 years imprisonment plus 100-300% penalty on evaded tax. Fraudulent input tax credit: criminal prosecution. Non-registration when required: 10% of tax due penalty.
exceptions: Petroleum products temporarily excluded from GST (still under state VAT)
Alcohol for human consumption exempt from GST
Threshold turnover exemption: businesses under ₹40 lakh exempt from registration

quiz.q: What governance innovation did India's GST introduce for tax rate decisions?
options: Tax rates are set by an independent judicial tribunal
The GST Council — comprising central and all state finance ministers — decides rates, requiring 3/4 majority — a cooperative federalism model
Tax rates are automatically adjusted based on inflation index
Parliament sets rates annually through Finance Bill with simple majority
quiz.explanation: The GST Council is a unique institution: it includes the Union Finance Minister plus all 28 state + 2 UT finance ministers, and decides GST rates by a three-quarter weighted majority (center has 1/3 weight; states combined have 2/3). This cooperative federalism model requires center-state consensus on tax policy — unprecedented in India's historically contested federal finance relations.

laws.title: Armed Forces Special Powers Act — AFSPA
laws.subtitle: Controversial military powers in disturbed areas of India
laws.fullDescription: India's Armed Forces Special Powers Act (1958, extended to J&K in 1990) grants the military extraordinary powers in 'disturbed areas': soldiers may fire on any person based on a belief they are violating law, arrest without warrant, enter and search without warrant, and destroy arms dumps. Crucially, prosecution of armed forces personnel requires central government sanction — nearly never granted in practice. AFSPA has been called a 'license to kill' by critics including the UN. The Manorama case (Manipur, 2004), where a woman was allegedly raped and killed in custody by Assam Rifles, triggered major protests. Supreme Court ruled (2016) that AFSPA does not give blanket immunity.
laws.penalty: AFSPA protects armed forces from prosecution without central government sanction (which is rarely given). Civilian compensation schemes exist but are seen as inadequate.
exceptions: AFSPA only applies in declared 'disturbed areas' — currently parts of Northeast India and Jammu & Kashmir
Regular police may not invoke AFSPA powers — only central armed forces
Human rights violations may still be investigated by NHRC though prosecution remains blocked
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Home Affairs — Government of India

quiz.q: What makes AFSPA uniquely controversial regarding accountability for military misconduct?
options: AFSPA allows civilians to sue military personnel personally for damages
Prosecution of armed forces under AFSPA requires central government sanction — which is almost never granted
AFSPA allows military to impose martial law without parliamentary approval
AFSPA transfers all judicial functions to military courts
quiz.explanation: AFSPA's core controversy: actions taken by armed forces in disturbed areas require central government sanction for prosecution — and the government virtually never grants this sanction. This creates de facto impunity for military conduct in AFSPA areas. The Supreme Court ruled in 2016 that AFSPA does not grant blanket immunity for encounter killings, but prosecutions remain extremely rare.

laws.title: National Green Tribunal Act, 2010
laws.subtitle: India's specialized environmental court
laws.fullDescription: India's National Green Tribunal (NGT) was established in 2010 as a specialized court for environmental disputes, combining technical expertise with judicial authority. The NGT has original jurisdiction over all environmental laws including the Environment Protection Act, Forest Conservation Act, Water Act, Air Act, and Biodiversity Act. The NGT ordered closure of 1,000+ industries polluting the Ganga. It banned diesel vehicles over 15 years old in Delhi. The NGT has been remarkably active: 44,000+ matters filed between 2011-2021. India's Supreme Court has reinforced NGT's authority. The Public Trust Doctrine — environmental resources held in trust for public — has been recognized.
laws.penalty: NGT orders carry full court authority. Non-compliance is contempt of court: up to 3 years imprisonment or ₹25 crore fine. States must comply within 3-month deadlines for remediation orders.
exceptions: High Courts retain concurrent jurisdiction on environmental matters
Central government decisions on forest diversion reviewed but not overridden in same way as state decisions
Activities by armed forces may be processed through government rather than NGT
laws.sourceLabel: National Green Tribunal — Government of India

quiz.q: What makes India's National Green Tribunal unusual among Indian courts?
options: It is the only court allowed to impose death penalty for environmental crimes
It combines technical experts with judges, giving it specialized environmental expertise beyond a regular court
It operates entirely online with no physical hearings
Its decisions can be appealed only to the UN Environment Programme
quiz.explanation: The NGT is unusual in its composition: it includes judicial members (judges) plus expert members with technical backgrounds in environmental sciences, economics, administrative management — combining legal authority with scientific expertise. This allows the court to evaluate complex scientific evidence without purely relying on expert witnesses, making environmental judgments more technically informed.

laws.title: Unlawful Activities Prevention Act — UAPA
laws.subtitle: India's anti-terrorism law with broad designation powers
laws.fullDescription: India's Unlawful Activities Prevention Act (UAPA, 1967, amended 2019) allows designation of individuals as terrorists (not just organizations) without trial. The 2019 amendment allows NIA to attach property of designated terrorists. UAPA cases have extremely low bail rates — courts are reluctant to grant bail given the statutory bar unless there are reasonable grounds to believe the accused is not guilty. High-profile UAPA arrests: journalists, academics, social activists, human rights defenders. The Bhima Koregaon case involved UAPA arrests of 16 academics, lawyers, and activists — Supreme Court took extraordinary step of staying NIA's claimed digital evidence after cybersecurity experts alleged it was planted.
laws.penalty: Membership in terrorist organization: up to life imprisonment. Terrorist acts causing death: death penalty or life. Funding terrorism: up to 10 years. Bail extremely restricted — almost impossible to obtain pending trial.
exceptions: Protected speech on purely academic study of terrorist ideologies
Journalism covering terrorist activities with journalistic intent
Official government negotiations with designated groups in peace processes
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Home Affairs — Government of India

quiz.q: What controversial power did India's 2019 UAPA amendment add?
options: Courts can now convict based solely on intelligence reports
Individuals (not just organizations) can be designated as terrorists without trial
UAPA now applies to foreign nationals who have never visited India
Death penalty made mandatory for all UAPA offenses
quiz.explanation: The 2019 UAPA amendment allowed designation of individuals as 'terrorists' without conviction or trial — previously only organizations could be designated. This means someone can be officially labeled a terrorist and have property seized without being convicted, or sometimes even charged, with any offense. Critics say this enables stigmatization without due process; supporters say it is necessary for financial disruption of terror networks.

laws.title: Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana — Financial Inclusion
laws.subtitle: India's mission to bank the unbanked 500 million
laws.fullDescription: Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY, 2014) is the world's largest financial inclusion program, opening 500+ million zero-balance bank accounts for previously unbanked Indians. Combined with Aadhaar (biometric ID) and mobile (phone), the JAM Trinity (Jan Dhan-Aadhaar-Mobile) enabled direct benefit transfers — eliminating corruption-prone subsidy intermediaries. DBT (Direct Benefit Transfer) has saved ₹2.7+ lakh crore ($32B+) by eliminating ghost beneficiaries. PMJDY accounts come with accidental insurance (₹2 lakh) and overdraft facility. India's UPI (Unified Payments Interface) built on this infrastructure now processes $2 trillion+ annually and is being exported to other countries.
laws.penalty: Bank fraud using PMJDY accounts: criminal prosecution under IPC/BNS. Identity fraud using Aadhaar for DBT: up to 3 years imprisonment under Aadhaar Act.
exceptions: Zero-balance requirement means no minimum balance penalty
Dormant accounts (2+ years inactive) converted to 'basic savings account' with limited transactions
Non-residents can hold NRE/NRO accounts under Foreign Exchange Management Act
laws.sourceLabel: Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana — Government of India

quiz.q: What is India's 'JAM Trinity' and why is it significant for policy delivery?
options: JAM refers to the Judiciary-Administration-Military triangle of Indian governance
Jan Dhan accounts + Aadhaar biometric ID + Mobile phones — enabling direct cash transfer to 500M+ people, eliminating corruption
Joint Audit Mechanism for checking government contractor fraud
quiz.explanation: The JAM Trinity (Jan Dhan-Aadhaar-Mobile) enables government benefits to be transferred directly to verified beneficiaries' bank accounts — bypassing corrupt intermediaries who previously skimmed subsidies. By linking bank accounts to biometric Aadhaar ID and mobile phones, India eliminated ghost beneficiaries and leakage, saving an estimated $32+ billion. This technology-enabled welfare delivery model is being studied globally.

laws.title: Foreign Contribution Regulation Act — FCRA
laws.subtitle: India's restrictions on foreign funding of civil society
laws.fullDescription: India's Foreign Contribution Regulation Act (FCRA, 2010, amended 2020) requires NGOs and civil society organizations to obtain FCRA registration to receive foreign donations. The 2020 amendment: prohibited transfer of foreign contributions to other organizations, reduced permissible administrative expenses from 50% to 20% of foreign contributions, and required all foreign contributions to be received only in designated SBI accounts. Major organizations losing FCRA registration: Greenpeace India, Amnesty International India, Missionaries of Charity (Mother Teresa's organization, temporarily). Critics say FCRA is used to silence government critics; government says it prevents foreign interference.
laws.penalty: Receiving foreign contributions without FCRA registration: up to 5 years imprisonment. Violation of FCRA terms: up to 5 years. Assets acquired through illegal foreign contributions confiscated.
exceptions: Political parties may not receive any foreign contributions (including from NRIs under certain structures)
Journalists and media entities receiving foreign press payments have separate treatment
Academic institutions receiving foreign scholarship/fellowship funds have modified requirements
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Home Affairs — FCRA Division

quiz.q: What major organizations lost FCRA registration in India after the 2020 amendments?
options: All foreign-owned companies operating in India
Greenpeace India, Amnesty International India, and briefly Missionaries of Charity (Mother Teresa's organization)
All foreign universities offering degrees in India
International law firms providing legal services to Indian NGOs
quiz.explanation: The 2020 FCRA amendments led to cancellation or suspension of registrations of prominent civil society groups: Greenpeace India (ended India operations), Amnesty International India (suspended operations citing government hostility), and briefly Mother Teresa's Missionaries of Charity (registration temporarily cancelled over alleged 'foreign origin' funds, restored after international attention). The pattern led critics to argue FCRA is being weaponized against government critics.
